Abyssal Corrosion Syndrome (also: Abyss Corrosion Syndrome, Draught of Lucidity): Abyssal Corrosion Syndrome is an illness caused by direct contact with high concentrations of Abyssal power. It harms body and mind, can leave irreversible mental trauma, and mostly appears as hallucinations. It is named in Natlan during the Abyssal invasion. The worst cases are treated with the Draught of Lucidity.

The name is given by "The Captain" (Capitano) in the Archon Quest interlude "For the Same Land." Iansan later keeps patient records of the many people she finds affected.

In universe: Symptoms include psychosis, often with sight and sound hallucinations and the reliving of past traumas. Severity follows the patient's level of trauma. In "For the Same Land," Atoco relives a childhood near-drowning, and Cochitta's fear of losing her loved ones is triggered by the memory of her parents' deaths.

Mild cases keep some awareness of the outside world and can be broken out of the hallucination by speaking to the person and by physical contact. Deep cases, such as the warrior Ocotlan, are lost in the hallucination and respond only to medicine.

Treatment: Verbal and physical contact for light cases; the Draught of Lucidity for severe ones.

The draught dispels the psychological effects of the Abyss, but its side effects are severe, including chronic migraines for life. It is therefore reserved for the worst cases. It was made for humans and also works on saurians.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): portray a patient as sincere but locked in the past, answering people who are not there. Treat the draught as a harsh remedy, not a casual cure. Gentle talk and touch are canon for mild cases.

1.comment: Abyssal Corrosion Syndrome: Draught of Lucidity
1.content: A medicine developed by the Khaenri'ahn military doctor Guthred to treat Abyssal Corrosion Syndrome. It dispels the psychological impact of the Abyss but can cause chronic migraines for life, so it is used only for severe cases. It works on saurians as well as humans.

2.content:
Adeptal Arts (also: Adeptus Arts, adeptal power, adeptal energy, arts of the adepti, adeptal techniques): The Adeptal Arts are the techniques of Liyue's adepti, the illuminated beasts and gods led by Rex Lapis (Morax). They include alchemy for making elixirs, paper sigils that store adeptal power, the creation of pocket-world abodes, and dream arts. The power is generally harmful or lethal to ordinary mortals, and the adepti guard their methods closely.

Rex Lapis is said to have taught these arts to the adepti. Their elemental abilities come with them, since all adepti can command elemental energy. Mortals who learn a technique do not become adepti.

In universe: Adepti can manipulate elemental energy without a Vision, which is why Liyue's people call them the "three-eyed" mighty and illuminated adepti; their Visions, when worn, are shown as a human convention. Beyond that, each adeptus carries adeptal energy with an effect particular to them, which is dangerous to mortals who spend too long near it.

Core techniques named in canon:
- Alchemy (Dandi), used to refine elixirs. The item text on the Mist Veiled Mercury Elixir says that anyone who swallows an elixir meets certain death, since the power in them is lethal to non-adepti.
- Sigils (Fulu), paper talismans that hold adeptal power as symbols.
- Sub-Space Creation (Waijing), the making of autonomous pocket worlds through imagination. Rex Lapis granted this ability.
- Dream Trawler, the giving and receiving of dreams.
- Mortal Lingering, taking a temporary human form after the original body has died.
- The Nuo Dance of Evil Conquering, a yaksha technique that uses the power of a yaksha mask (see System: Karma).

Alchemy and elixirs: Adeptal alchemy produces elixirs of great power that kill mortals who swallow them. The Mist Veiled Mercury Elixir is the item the game uses to describe this, and the Mist Veiled Gold Elixir is known for giving weapons transcendent powers. Remedium Tertiorum, a medicine Zhongli once offered for Xiao, temporarily eases the pain of karma and follows the same rule: in his words, nothing of this world can withstand it.

Sigils: Sigils (Fulu) store adeptal power in symbols and typically appear as paper talismans. Qiqi wears talismans that hold in the adeptal power inside her body; without them, her profile says it would send her into a berserk state.

Abodes and dreams: Sub-Space Creation lets an adeptus build a small pocket world, usually a home for themselves. Madame Ping's teapot and the Serenitea Pot are examples; larger abodes such as the Realm of Clouds and the Sea Gazer's Abode were made the same way. Adepti may also make teapot spirits to run an abode, and the spirits receive adeptus names.

Adeptal energy and mortals: Adeptal energy gives each adeptus a particular effect. In Turning Point, when the Traveler was lent power from Madame Ping, Ganyu and Xiao, Ping's gave shockwaves with attacks, Ganyu's gave healing and Xiao's gave extra speed. Ordinary mortals cannot endure too much of it: their souls are not as robust, and with enough time it overwhelms them.

Devices and compass: Adepti have also put their arts into devices. Cloud Retainer (Xianyun) believes the laws of nature can be invested in ingenious devices, so she builds mechanisms for the people of Liyue; Zibai notes that she would rather tinker than use her powers. The Fantastic Compass, made by the adeptus Sea Gazer to seal away monsters, is a catalyst that shines when an adeptus and a mortal use it together.

Limits: Adeptal power harms mortals and is not given freely. Humans can learn some adeptal arts, but they do not become adepti, since canon applies the word to non-humans (half-humans can qualify).

Adeptal abilities do not remove limits: the Serenitea Pot cannot hold a city, and not even Sub-Space Creation can restore Padisarah flowers that died out when the Goddess of Flowers fell. Dream arts and sigils take effort and are often kept secret from the public.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): adeptal-themed content includes the Serenitea Pot realm, adeptal-themed furnishings, the Mist Veiled elixirs as weapon-ascension materials, adeptal-themed talents such as Qiqi's Adeptus Art: Preserver of Fortune, and Xiao's Bane of All Evil.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show adeptal power as quiet and costly rather than flashy. A simple talisman glow, a hush, a chill or warmth in the air, or a hint of old incense fits. Adepti guard their methods, so a character who asks about the arts should usually get a partial or indirect answer.

3.content: Waijing is the adeptal ability to build small, self-contained pocket worlds through imagination. Rex Lapis granted it, and it has been used for abodes: Madame Ping's teapot, Cloud Retainer's Realm of Clouds, Sea Gazer's Abode and the Serenitea Pot. The result is not a true world and cannot hold a whole city, but its energy can make soil fertile and water warm and clear. Adepti also make teapot spirits to manage these homes.

4.content: A talisman made by Rex Lapis and charged with adeptal power. In the Archon War mortals used such sigils to channel power in battle; by the present most of the power has worn off, yet adepti will not harm a holder, and a holder is said to be able to enter Jueyun Karst without offending them. The Fatui copied the design and used the copies to briefly free Osial during the Archon Quest.

5.content: A catalyst made by the adeptus Sea Gazer to seal away monsters, later passed to a human friend and used to exorcise demons together. In the cataclysm, Bosacius and Boyang used it to seal the Chasm's Bed. Its power needs both an adeptus and a mortal; Yanfei, who has both ancestries, can briefly wake it.

6.content:
Aggravate (also: Aggravate reaction, Electro Catalyze reaction): Aggravate is the Electro half of the Catalyze family. First an Electro hit and a Dendro hit meet and put a Quicken aura on the target; after that, further Electro hits on the Quickened target trigger Aggravate, which makes each of them hit harder by a flat amount. It is a combat rule rather than a story event, and the reaction arrived with Version 3.0.

Aggravate does not consume the Quicken aura, so it can fire again and again until the aura runs out. Dendro attacks on the same aura trigger Spread instead, which gives a larger bonus.

In universe: Canon presents Aggravate only through the Elemental Trial tutorial and gameplay text. The wiki records that the Electro and Dendro reaction is said to have a deep connection to the history of Sumeru, but no source read for this entry explains how.

Any link between Electro and Dendro in Sumeru's past, including claims about Nabu Malikata, is inference by wiki editors, not stated canon. Keep scenes from asserting one.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): an Electro attack on a target with a Quicken aura triggers Aggravate and adds an Additive Base DMG Bonus to that attack's damage. Aggravate does not consume the aura.

The bonus is 1.15 times the level multiplier of the character, increased by a percentage from Elemental Mastery and any Reaction DMG Bonus, and then added to the attack's base damage before the usual damage bonuses, CRIT, DEF and RES. Spread is the Dendro version, with coefficient 1.25.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show a Quickened target as crackling with green-violet energy, so that each Electro strike lands with extra bite as lightning bites into the growing charge. Keep it a rising intensity, not a new effect.

Limits: Aggravate needs an existing Quicken aura and an Electro attack that can apply Electro; Dendro attacks trigger Spread instead.

The bonus belongs to the attack that triggers it, so Aggravate does nothing on its own and adds nothing to a skill that deals no damage.

7.content: Aggravate is the Electro Catalyze reaction (Version 3.0). An Electro attack on a Quickened target gains a flat damage bonus without using up the Quicken aura.

8.content:
Alchemy (also: alchemist arts, Bio-Alchemy, biological alchemy): Alchemy in Teyvat is the art of transmuting and combining matter. In its everyday form it mends, brews and refines; at its peak it can reshape living things, even create them. Mondstadt practises it openly (the Knights of Favonius employ a Chief Alchemist, Albedo), Sumeru's Akademiya studies it in its Spantamad Darshan, Liyue's adepti keep a private version, and Snezhnaya forbids it. The pinnacle is Khaenri'ah's Art of Khemia, which creates life and is tied to the Cataclysm.

This entry covers alchemy as a whole. The Art of Khemia has its own entry, as do individual characters such as Albedo and Sucrose. The same word also names the game's crafting system, which is only a loose reflection of the lore (see gameplay).

In universe: Alchemy is a body of techniques for transforming materials and living things by controlled processes: potions, solutions, transmutation arrays, cauldrons. It does not require a Vision; Sucrose received hers in the middle of an alchemy experiment, not before it. Alchemy comes in levels: ordinary alchemy is limited, while the deepest forms touch the nature of life itself.

Albedo's Character Details say that, to most Mondstadters, alchemy meant little more than mending broken odds and ends, until Albedo arrived and showed what it can do, bringing a corpus of knowledge the Sumeru Akademiya did not have. He describes dust as the most basic form of complex life and demonstrated this by growing a Cecilia from the burnt ash of a flower. The sub-categories most often named are bio-alchemy (modifying or transforming existing life), the Art of Khemia (creating new life) and, in Sumeru, alchemical divination and potion-craft.

Mondstadt: Mondstadt practises alchemy openly. The Knights of Favonius count a Chief Alchemist among their ranks; Albedo holds that post, with Sucrose and Timaeus as his assistants. Sucrose practises bio-alchemy, working to modify existing life.

Albedo came to Mondstadt with a recommendation letter from his master Rhinedottir, addressed to Alice, who placed him with the Knights of Favonius, believing they could provide the large laboratory he needed. He prefers fundamental questions: the nature of things and the creation of life. Sucrose's interest runs the other way: using alchemy to modify existing life and add variety and colour to the world. Her results include a special potion that raised the nectar output of Sweet Flowers by 70 percent and a spray that keeps Sunsettias fresh for a month; she treats these as incidental steps toward a larger, still secret, goal.

Liyue: Liyue's adepti practise their own alchemy, a closely guarded secret that most people do not know exists. The adepti use it to make elixirs. Item text for the Mist Veiled Mercury Elixir says the power in these elixirs is lethal to anyone who is not an adeptus, and the wiki records that Mist Veiled Gold Elixir text says such elixirs can give weapons transcendent power.

Sumeru: At the Sumeru Akademiya, alchemy is one of the fields of the Spantamad Darshan, which specialises in subjects connected with ley lines and the elements. Some scholars of the Amurta Darshan are also skilled in potion-craft.

Khaenriah: The Art of Khemia is Khaenri'ah's form of alchemy. Because Khaenri'ah was an underground nation with little natural life, it focused on creating life, and it began as a way to make plants grow without sunlight. It later grew advanced enough to create far more complex beings, and it contributed to the nation's downfall in the Cataclysm 500 years ago. See its own entry for the details.

Snezhnaya: Snezhnaya once practised alchemy freely under the Belyi Tsar, and later banned it. The Tsaritsa now forbids the populace from using alchemy, and the Harbingers enforce the ban. The wiki connects the old freedom to the creation of the Aberrant Chimeric Monsters, which alchemists made by recklessly combining forms of life.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Alchemy is a crafting system used at a Crafting Bench. It combines three lower-tier materials with Mora to make one higher-tier material, and it also produces some potions and gadgets such as Condensed Resin. Adventure Rank unlocks certain recipes.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show alchemy as patient, hands-on process: weighing, dissolving, simmering, chalked arrays, cauldron steam and notebooks of failed trials. Mondstadt alchemists are scholars, not villains; their danger is curiosity, not malice. A Snezhnayan scene should treat alchemy as forbidden and spoken of carefully.

Limits: Canon never lists exactly what alchemy cannot do. It is shown as skilled, not omnipotent: Sucrose's experiments often fail (her Vision came from one that burned her dandelion seeds to a crisp), and the Remelting Effect and alchemical divination have narrow uses.

9.content: Bio-alchemy focuses on changing existing life. In Mondstadt its practitioners are Sucrose and, according to the wiki, Rhinedottir; Sucrose most likely learned it from Albedo. Sucrose uses it to improve plants and preservation, not to create new beings. Snezhnaya's bio-alchemists, such as Koshchei, went much further and were suppressed.

10.content: The Aberrant Chimeric Monsters are an enemy group found in Snezhnaya. The Adventure Handbook calls them creations of the biological alchemy that once flourished there before it was forbidden. They were made in the Belyi Tsar's reign by alchemists, above all Koshchei, who combined many forms of life. Most were consumed in the war against the Onslaught of Dark Beasts, and the few survivors are rare and dangerous. Named types include the Chimeric Armored Beast, Burrowbeast, Winged Elephant, Horned Bear and Winged Lion, and the Immortal Construct.

11.content: Two Sumeru alchemies from Spantamad: alchemical divination (reading the ashes from a failed transmutation, said to have been invented by Lesser Lord Kusanali) and the Remelting Effect, which uses explosive Remelting Tablets invented by Hajanad. Both appear in Akademiya-related quests.

12.content:
Anemo (also: Anemo element, element of wind): Anemo is the element of wind, one of Teyvat's seven elements. Its Archon is Barbatos, who lives in Mondstadt as the bard Venti; Mondstadt is the nation of wind and freedom. People with Anemo Visions raise gusts and updrafts, pull or push things with vortices, and glide on the wind. The Anemo Dragon Sovereign is Dvalin, once called Stormterror. The Harbinger Signora took the Anemo Gnosis from Venti for the Tsaritsa.

Neuvillette calls Barbatos "the God of Breeze and Hope." Anemo ascension gems are Vayuda Turquoise.

In universe: Most people cannot use Anemo. Those who can usually hold an Anemo Vision. Venti draws on the Anemo Authority of his divine throne in Celestia instead; the "Vision" on his hip is, in his words, "a glowing glass ball I carry around to avoid suspicion."

Legend says that after Barbatos became Archon about 2,600 years ago, he blew away the ice and snow left by the Archon War, scattered mountains, flattened cliffs into plains and guided warm monsoons into Mondstadt. Legend also credits his blessing with making the first wind gliders fly. Mondstadters call their wine a "gift from the Anemo Archon."

Archon and nation: Archon: Barbatos (Venti), the God of Freedom, who with Morax is one of the two surviving original members of The Seven. Nation: Mondstadt, which he deliberately leaves to govern itself.

He became Archon about 2,600 years ago after the rebellion against Decarabian, the God of Storms, then withdrew from rule for fear of becoming a tyrant. Few Mondstadters know that the bard Venti is their god. Venti calls himself the weakest Archon, because Archons draw power from how much control they hold over their nations.

Gnosis and authority: In Ending Note (Prologue, 1.0), Signora ambushed a weakened Venti and pulled the Anemo Gnosis from his chest. A Gnosis, Venti explained, is an Archon's internal focus that resonates directly with Celestia. Later canon shows that Archons keep their divine thrones and their elemental power without a Gnosis.

Elemental beings: Dvalin, the Anemo Dragon Sovereign, and Anemo elemental lifeforms such as slimes, specters and the Anemo Hypostasis.

Dvalin, Dragon of the East, was born from a convergence of elemental energy in the high heavens and succeeded an unnamed, dead Anemo Sovereign. Anemo Samachurls are hilichurl shamans who command the winds.

Known uses: Gusts and updrafts, gliding, whirlwinds that gather foes or debris, and pushing things away. Anemo also scatters other elements.

Anemo also raises barriers: Decarabian's storm wall resisted even Boreas, and a storm barrier sealed Stormterror's Lair in the Prologue. It can sharpen the senses: Kazuha reads the sounds of nature to sense rain or snow from a single gust.

Limits: Anemo does not react with Geo or Dendro.

Swirl spreads an element that is already present; it does not create one. A Vision fixes its holder to one element: Kazuha's brief Electro use came from a second, borrowed Vision.

Interactions: Swirl: when Anemo meets Pyro, Hydro, Electro or Cryo it spreads that element to nearby targets (own entry).

Elemental Absorption: many Anemo skills take on Pyro, Hydro, Electro or Cryo on first contact and deal that element's damage as well.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Anemo is a damage type and the element of characters such as Venti, Jean, Sucrose, Xiao, Kaedehara Kazuha, the Wanderer and Xianyun.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show Anemo as pressure, sound and motion: cloaks snapping, grass flattening in a ring, dust spiralling. Teal or aqua-green light is a safe cue; Venti's braids glow Anemo-aqua when he uses his power. Keep scale proportionate: a Vision holder can knock people down or glide from a cliff, but reshaping mountains is an Archon's work.

13.content: The Anemo Dragon Sovereign today is Dvalin, who succeeded an earlier, unnamed Anemo dragon who died before the game's events. Dvalin was born from a convergence of elemental energy in the high heavens and drawn to Barbatos's lyre. He became the Dragon of the East of the Four Winds after Vennessa's rebellion.

14.content: Anemoculi are consolidated winds found across Mondstadt. According to The Blessings of The Seven, only allogenes and the Traveler can see them. They are offered at Statues of The Seven, which legend says once had gem eyes that swallows carried off, in exchange for The Seven's blessing. Item text describes the Anemoculus as a substance "that has accumulated intense Anemo energy", offered to help a statue regain power it has lost.

15.content:
Archaeolune Energy (also: Archaeolune, ancient moon energy, ancient moon's power, Blue Kuuvahki, Moonvein Suffusion, Archaeolune Ripples): Archaeolune Energy is an ancient, primordial power found on the Frost Moon, the one intact moon above Nod-Krai. It is closely tied to kuuvahki, the moonlight-power of Nod-Krai, and is considered kuuvahki's primordial form; characters in the story usually call it "ancient moon energy". It fills the moon's core, powers the dragon-built machines on the moon, and can create life. It first appeared in the Moon Gazing quests (Version 6.7).

In game terms it is the basis of exploration on the Frost Moon: absorbing it puts the Traveler into a state called Moonvein Suffusion, which makes the body lighter and jumps higher and lets them fire Archaeolune Ripples. The wiki reports that Columbina simply calls it "Blue Kuuvahki".

In universe: Kuuvahki, the power of the Three Moons, is a primordial form of elemental energy that belongs to the Light Realm. Columbina says kuuvahki and the ancient moon's energy are both, in essence, the power of the Light Realm. The wiki describes Archaeolune Energy as the primordial form of kuuvahki that shares the properties of two other primordial energies: phlogiston (programmable matter, an energy source, and a medium for storing and recording information) and the Primordial Sea (the power of creation, including the creation of life).

Dragon-era engineers built facilities on the moon around it. Pioneer Source Structures, said to be constructs of the dragons of Natlantea, store it. Ancient Moon Pearls are spherical energy vessels, pearl power stations feed it through energy pathways to doors and machines, and Archaeolune Energy Barriers guard dragon facilities linked to the moons. A deep base on the moon is powered by a stream of the energy rising from a fissure that leads to the moon's core. Eggie explains that this base was meant to turn the moon into a space-based weapon; Columbina describes it as the work of the returning dragon king Nibelung, who reforged the moon into a weapon whose core energy would become artillery fire aimed at Teyvat. That ruler was defeated by the Heavenly Principles, and Columbina says the site is no longer a threat.

Dangers: Archaeolune Storms. When the lunar sea beneath Ungien's Circle is disturbed, highly concentrated energy leaks out as an Archaeolune Storm, which Columbina says harms all living beings other than kuuhenki. An occlusion field can temporarily hold the storms back. Blue areas of high concentration are best avoided.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore). Absorbing Archaeolune Energy from a source puts the Traveler in the Moonvein Suffusion state, which raises jump height, grants Archaeolune Ripples, and (per the wiki, flagged for verification) after a certain point in Pioneers (Part 2) also grants Moonlight Dash charges. Sources: Ancient Moon Pearls, Archaeolune Energy Nodes, Archaeolune Energy Surges, Pioneer Source Structures that are not on alert, and Wondrous Black Kuuhenki.

Limits: Pearls cannot move once packed into a container, and barriers regenerate shortly after a hole is made. The energy is not one of the seven elements, and canon gives it no Vision or elemental reactions. Pioneer Source Structures can be drained only when not on alert, and then power back up after a short time.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text). Archaeolune Energy is quiet and cold: blue-lit machinery, floating stones, slow falls and a faint sense of lightness. It belongs to the Frost Moon, not to ordinary Teyvat, and outsiders should treat it as unfamiliar and potentially harmful in high concentration.

16.content: Moonvein Suffusion is the gameplay state entered by absorbing an object filled with Archaeolune Energy: the body feels lighter and jumps are higher, and the player can fire Archaeolune Ripples that detonate to damage objects and alter their gravity. The wiki notes that Moonlight Dash, which turns the player into a black kuuhenki for fast movement, is also granted after a certain quest step. Pressing the Elemental Burst button exits the state.

17.content: Ancient Moon Pearls are energy vessels for Archaeolune Energy, found on the Frost Moon and in Dunanna Pit. Their loading-screen description calls them wondrous spherical devices that roll, whose true function is to store energy. Pushing a pearl into a power station transfers its energy, which flows along pathways to power machinery; a launcher can throw a pearl (or a standing character) to a distant spot. Pioneer Source Structures, built by the dragons of Natlantea according to the wiki, are fed by the same energy and have modules for edict, stasis, transmission and annihilation.

18.content: An Archaeolune Storm is a surge of highly concentrated ancient moon energy that spreads when the lunar sea at the moon's core is disturbed. Columbina says it harms all living beings other than kuuhenki. Eggie notes that an occlusion field can hold such storms back for a while, and that the facility beneath Ungien's Circle draws its power from the lunar sea.

19.content:
Arkhe (also: Pneuma, Ousia, Pneumousia, Pneuma and Ousia, Pneuma-Ousia Annihilation, Arkhe alignment): Arkhe is a pair of opposing energies native to Fontaine: Pneuma and Ousia. When one meets the other, the two annihilate and release a greater burst of energy. This Pneuma-Ousia Annihilation is what powers most of Fontaine's Clockwork Meka. Arkhe is not one of the seven elements. It is a separate, Fontaine-specific energy, and most Fontainian characters carry one alignment of it.

The two names are often joined as "Pneumousia" in Fontaine's engineering and environment text. A hit of one alignment on something charged with the other disrupts it, so a machine's own power supply can be turned against it.

In universe: In-game tutorials describe Pneuma and Ousia as properties found in the life-forms, earth, air and watery veins of Fontaine. When energies of different properties collide they annihilate and yield greater energy. This is the principle that powers many Clockwork Meka.

Meka power supplies are unstable and settle into a Pneuma-aligned or Ousia-aligned state. An attack of the opposite alignment overloads the supply and disables the machine for a time. Combat-oriented meka keep a backup system for low-end fighting, while utility meka lose their combat functions entirely.

Character alignment: Most Fontainian characters, and the Hydro Traveler, have an innate Arkhe alignment, reflected in the shape of their Vision. Pneuma belongs to Neuvillette, Lyney, Freminet, Charlotte and Emilie, and to the Hydro Traveler. Ousia belongs to Navia, Clorinde, Wriothesley, Sigewinne, Lynette, Chevreuse and Escoffier. Furina is listed under both and can alternate between the two.

Known uses: Disabling Clockwork Meka by striking with the opposite alignment, solving Fontaine puzzles, and stunning Breacher Primuses in their stressed state.

Pneumousia Blocks found in the wild can be picked up and released on the next attack. The underwater tutorial notes that most Fontainian characters can trigger their own alignment underwater without blocks. Enhanced Pneumousia Amplifiers apply an elemental aura to nearby enemies, and an opposite-Arkhe hit disables one for the rest of the fight.

Limits: Arkhe is not an element and does not react like one.

An Arkhe hit does not apply elemental effects. Annihilation needs two opposite alignments; matching alignments do nothing special.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Arkhe is a combat and exploration mechanic introduced in Version 4.0. Pneuma and Ousia talents trigger on a fixed Arkhe interval, and some weapons have passives that depend on Arkhe alignment. While diving, a character's attacks default to their own alignment, since they have no access to their combat talents.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): treat Arkhe as a Fontainian thing, a quiet hum of mutual opposition. Pneuma reads as sharp, thorn-like and spirit-like; Ousia reads as heavy, surging and substantial, echoing the in-game thorn and blade effects. Keep it distinct from elemental power: a Fontainian can have a Vision element and an Arkhe alignment at once.

20.content: Pneuma is one of the two Arkhe energies. In gameplay it appears as the Spiritbreath Thorn follow-up and as white-clockwork meka. Characters aligned with Pneuma include Neuvillette, Lyney, Freminet, Charlotte, Emilie and the Hydro Traveler, and Furina can use Pneuma as well. A Pneuma meka is weakened by an Ousia hit.

21.content: Ousia is the other Arkhe energy. In gameplay it appears as the Surging Blade follow-up and as dark-blue-clockwork meka. Characters aligned with Ousia include Navia, Clorinde, Wriothesley, Sigewinne, Lynette, Chevreuse and Escoffier, and Furina can use Ousia as well. An Ousia meka is weakened by a Pneuma hit.

22.content: Pneumousia Blocks are energy blocks found in Fontaine's wilderness, in Pneuma and Ousia varieties. Once picked up, the next Normal, Charged or Plunging attack releases the stored energy, including underwater. Alain Guillotin is credited with inventing artificial blocks over 400 years ago, which he used to power his meka. Blocks also let meka run outside Fontaine, though only briefly.

23.content: When Pneuma and Ousia meet, they annihilate and produce a greater energy. Fontainian engineering harnesses this in controlled form inside kinetic cores, and it can overload an opposite-aligned meka. Fontaine Research Institute researchers found Arkhium's energy potential to be far greater than this reaction's.

24.content:
Arkhium (also: Arkhium crystal, Arkhium ore, Arkhium Kinetic Core, Arkhium Stock, Arkhium Lumenite): Arkhium is a yellow, green and blue crystalline ore that occurs in parts of Fontaine and works as an extremely potent energy source. The Fontaine Research Institute tried to use it to counter gravity so that a "city in the sky" could ride out the prophesied flood. A mechanical malfunction overloaded the Arkhium Kinetic Core, and the explosion destroyed much of the old Institute grounds.

Arkhium is distinct from Arkhe, the Pneuma and Ousia energy pair, though the Institute's researchers compared the two. Its energy potential far surpasses the controlled Pneuma-Ousia Annihilation reactions that power Clockwork Meka.

Properties: Arkhium separates matter, or certain things outside of matter, according to archive text; the separation can apparently be reversed, though there has been little interest in doing so. It is either inert, stable and giving off no energy, or activated, unstable and emitting powerful pulses.

Inert Arkhium can be activated in a catalytic environment, and activated Arkhium can be made inert with a specialised inhibitor. Activated crystals can set off a resonance that activates other crystals in range, risking an explosive chain reaction. After enough activation, a crystal's energy-generating potential runs out and it becomes permanently inert.

Fontaine research institute: The Fontaine Research Institute became interested in Arkhium because its energy potential far exceeded Pneuma-Ousia Annihilation. The goal was to counteract gravity and build a city in the sky so that Fontaine's people could survive the prophesied flood. Another proposed use was a ship lift at Romaritime Harbor. The Arkhium Research Project was led by Edwin Eastinghouse, a senior researcher specialising in Arkhium and gravimeters, with Nacker and Raimondo as collaborators.

Locations: Arkhium occurs naturally in parts of Fontaine, such as the Geode Mine Shaft beneath the Fortress of Meropide, which holds an inert vein. The ruined Central Laboratory Ruins, with their floating water cubes, mark where the Institute's core exploded.

Quest items: A world-quest chain has the Traveler gather seven Mysterious Ore pieces across Fontaine, which combine into Arkhium Stock. Forged at Bravais' Press Works, the stock becomes Arkhium Lumenite, which powers a door mechanism for the hidden objective "Arkhium Forge".

Limits: Arkhium is not a Vision element, and not the same thing as Arkhe.

Canon does not explain its origin or why it is concentrated at particular sites. It is dangerous without protection, and a depleted crystal is permanently dead.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): present Arkhium as an unstable laboratory hazard, with a dull buzz, warm glow and a sense of restrained danger, and as something researchers handle with detectors, inhibitors and nerves rather than bravado. Researchers might talk about "resonance", "inhibitors" and "radiation levels".

25.content: The Arkhium Kinetic Core was a concentrated energy source built around a large chunk of Arkhium ore, developed by Edwin Eastinghouse and Raimondo with a suppression device to control it. It fed the Experimental Field Generator. Its overload caused the explosion that destroyed much of the Fontaine Research Institute.

26.content: The Experimental Field Generator is a huge device created by Edwin Eastinghouse that produces a Gravity Reduction Field. The wiki lists the machine as Prototype Cal. Breguet, a Clockwork Meka. In combat the field greatly raises jump height, and three Pneuma-aligned hits end it.

27.content: Large cubes of water suspended in the sky around the Central Laboratory Ruins. They were created by the Arkhium explosion that destroyed the old Institute grounds.

28.content: A mine shaft beneath the Fortress of Meropide that contains a vein of inert Arkhium. Mining there ended after the Institute disaster. A Meropide inmate named Lechlade complains of headaches, palpitations and cold extremities near it, but the doctor dismisses this; it is unconfirmed whether this is exposure.

29.content: Edwin is a former Senior Technician of the Fontaine Research Institute, widely acknowledged as a genius and obsessively committed to research results, including at heavy cost to people. He led the Arkhium Research Project and built the Experimental Field Generator. He was presumed dead after the explosion; the Traveler later found him alive and still continuing Arkhium work, and he was fired and sent to the Fortress of Meropide.

30.content:
Art of Khemia (also: The Art of Khemia, Khaenri'ahn alchemy, Khemia): The Art of Khemia is the alchemy of Khaenri'ah. Because Khaenri'ah was an underground nation with little natural fauna, its alchemy centred on creating life, and it is quite different from the alchemy practised in the Seven Nations. Its master was "Gold" Rhinedottir, who made the dragon Durin, the synthetic human Albedo and many monsters. The Art played a major role in the fall of Khaenri'ah in the Cataclysm 500 years ago.

Albedo, Rhinedottir's creation and student, is the main living practitioner shown. Venti and Dainsleif, who were present at Khaenri'ah's fall, are uneasy about Albedo's use of it.

In universe: Khemia sits at the far end of alchemy: those who combine the pinnacle of alchemical skill with vast learning can create synthetic life, which Albedo calls the "apex achievement". Canon names only Rhinedottir as having reached that level. Its inner workings and history are not explained in canon.

Rhinedottir's demonstration to the young Albedo (Character Story 3) ties life to earth: the universe is the dark essence of the starry sky, the earth is the accumulated memories of time and lives, and the "chalk" is the one being taught. Albedo learned of the Art from his master's notes and was taught that after "soil" comes "chalk", the spotless soil used to make primordial man. His star-shaped neck mark is left where life force was sealed into his vessel; he compares it to a birthmark and to a pontil mark on blown glass.

History: The Art of Khemia grew in Khaenri'ah and was the alchemy that sustained the nation. Rhinedottir, an alchemist who served the Eclipse Dynasty in its closing years, became one of the Five Sinners of Khaenri'ah. Tempted by the Abyss, she took a share of the Abyssal power Irmin had given the Traveler's Sibling. Her monster armies then invaded Khaenri'ah and the seven nations in the Cataclysm.

Known creations: Durin (dragon), Albedo (synthetic human), the riftwolves, Elynas, the Bakunawa, Sebas and the False Horned Steed.

Rhinedottir called only two of her works "miraculous beings": Durin and Albedo. Durin terrorised Mondstadt's skies until Dvalin killed him over Dragonspine; Elynas polluted Fontaine until its armada wounded him fatally; the Bakunawa devoured the Tenochtzitoc tribe in Natlan before Tenoch and Sanhaj's sacrifice broke it apart.

Practitioners: Main practitioner: Rhinedottir (Gold). Her creation and student Albedo (Cretaceus) is the active practitioner. Sucrose (bio-alchemy) and Timaeus are Albedo's assistants and students but are not described as practising Khemia itself. Jakob Baker of the Narzissenkreuz Ordo is a possible practitioner: he researched alchemy extensively, with special interest in Khaenri'ahn Khemia and Rhinedottir's work.

Limits and cautions: Do not treat Khemia as ordinary Mondstadt alchemy or as a Vision power. It is not an element. It is slow, material and dangerous: Venti calls its power ancient and unmistakable and says he fears what would happen if someone lost control of it in the city.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show Khemia as quiet, exact craft, with chalk-drawn or glowing arrays, specimen notes, and a clinical calm. Its practitioners (Albedo especially) speak of creation as study, not conquest. Avoid portraying it as flashy combat magic.

31.content: Rhinedottir, called Gold, is a Khaenri'ahn alchemist, one of the Five Sinners of Khaenri'ah and a Hexenzirkel mage ("R"). She is the foremost known master of the Art of Khemia. After the Cataclysm she created Albedo and, after devouring the Heart of Naberius, took over Naberius's function as the Ruler of Life.

32.comment: Art of Khemia: Primordial Human Project
32.content: Rhinedottir's long project to create a human being through alchemy. Subject Two was an earlier failed result; Albedo, classed as Cretaceus, was the success. Albedo says the apex of alchemy is the creation of human life.

33.content:
Ascension Phase (also: character ascension, weapon ascension, ascending a character): Ascension Phase is a game-mechanics term: the number of times a character or weapon has been ascended. It determines the maximum level the character or weapon can reach; the highest phase, 6, allows level 90. It is not something characters experience in the story.

Each phase must be unlocked by reaching a required Adventure Rank (the player's account progress) and by spending materials. It has existed since version 1.0.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): ascending raises the level cap. Characters need level-up materials, enhancement materials and local specialties; weapons need weapon ascension materials and enhancement materials.

For characters, each Ascension Phase also unlocks new Passive Talents, raises the maximum level of Combat Talents, and unlocks further Character Stories and voice-overs in their profile. This is why a character's deeper backstory is revealed in stages in the game.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): do not have characters talk about their own "Ascension Phase" or "level 90". If a scene needs the idea, describe it as growth through training and experience. Do not conflate this mechanic with a mortal ascending to godhood, which is an in-world concept.

Limits: Applies to playable characters and weapons only; it has no canonical in-world explanation.

The cap of 6 phases and level 90 are the figures given for the mechanic as of 7.1; individual material costs are not recorded here.

34.content:
Azosite (also: Azosite energy, Azosite system, Azosite-powered system, Azosite smelting): Azosite is an ancient form of energy used by the Khaenri'ahns. It was made by extracting pure elemental energy from ley lines and smelting it into solid Energy Blocks, and it powered everything from ordinary ruin machines to large weapons-testing facilities. Over time the Khaenri'ahns found more effective sources, such as Abyssal energy, which gradually replaced it.

Azosite is described as convenient, stable and safe, but, in the view of a Fontainian researcher who studied it, lacking "will." Players first meet it in the Khaenri'ahn ruins beneath Sumeru's desert (Version 3.6).

In universe: The Khaenri'ahns refined elemental energy out of the ley lines and processed it into Energy Blocks. Azosite is not a separate force: notes found in the ruins say it is not fundamentally different from elemental energy and cannot break the rules that elemental energy must follow.

Because it is elemental energy, Azosite shares its properties, including the ability to reverse Abyssal influence. The same notes place the Abyss higher in the order of rules, since it can distort and pollute the elements of the gods. Energy Blocks fuel the backup power systems of Ruin Golems, and a quest item, the Mysterious Energy Block, is described in-game as a refined Azosite block formed by condensing pure elemental energy, usable for large-scale power systems.

History: The Khaenri'ahns used Azosite to power machines from common Ruin Guards up to sites such as Madinat al-Nuhas. Research from the Sumeru Akademiya suggests the technology may predate them: Jazari reports that Azosite power systems were probably in widespread use long before the first ruin machine was built in ancient Khaenri'ah, so the Khaenri'ahns need not have invented it.

Usage sites: Hangeh Afrasiyab, an abandoned underground factory in Gavireh Lajavard (Sumeru), was where Azosite was processed; a sealed gate to Khaenri'ah lies in its depths. In the quest "As the Khvarena's Light Shows," the Traveler and companions retrieved a Great Song of Khvarena there.

Limits: Azosite is pure elemental energy and so obeys the rules of elemental energy; it has no will of its own and sits beneath Abyssal power in the order of rules. Canon shows it only as Khaenri'ahn-era infrastructure and notes, not as a power anyone wields today.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): treat Azosite as old industrial infrastructure. Scenes can feature sealed smelting furnaces, stacked Energy Blocks, dim Ruin Golems on backup power, and worn engineers' notes. Scholars in Sumeru can plausibly discuss it as a curiosity from the Khaenri'ahn ruins.

35.content: Energy Blocks are solid, refined Azosite used to fuel the backup power systems of Ruin Golems. The Mysterious Energy Block is a quest item from "As the Khvarena's Light Shows: Nirodha," described as a block of refined Azosite formed by condensing pure elemental energy for large-scale power systems. The wiki also lists a Lost Energy Block as another form of Azosite.

36.content: An abandoned underground factory in Gavireh Lajavard where the Khaenri'ahns processed Azosite, described in notes as the last workshop in the kingdom with an entirely Azosite-powered system. A sealed gate to Khaenri'ah lies within, and the Traveler recovered a Great Song of Khvarena there in the quest "As the Khvarena's Light Shows."

37.content:
Bloom (also: Bloom reaction, Dendro Core, Dendro Cores, Bountiful Core, Bountiful Cores): Bloom is what happens when Dendro and Hydro meet on a target, in either order. The result is a Dendro Core: a small bud-like object that sits on the field for a few seconds and then bursts in a spray of Dendro damage around it. It arrived in Version 3.0 with the Dendro element.

A Dendro Core can also be hit with a third element before it bursts. Pyro turns it into Burgeon, a bigger blast. Electro turns it into Hyperbloom, a homing projectile (Sprawling Shot). Both are summarised below and have their own entries.

In universe: Canon offers no in-world explanation. Bloom is shown in tutorials and combat, not discussed by characters in the sources read. Treat it as a gameplay abstraction: a scene may borrow its look (a seed forming from water and verdant energy) but should not present a named in-world law.

Related setting: Dendro is the element associated with Sumeru. The wiki also notes that creatures made of Dendro, the Tri-Lakshana creatures, react with Hydro and Electro as Bloom and Quicken.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Dendro applied to a Hydro-affected target, or Hydro applied to a Dendro-affected one, creates a Dendro Core. It lasts up to 6 seconds. If it expires while the character who made it is still in the party and alive, it explodes for area Dendro damage in a 5 m radius, hurting enemies and players alike. Otherwise it simply disappears.

- At most 5 Dendro Cores exist at once; making a sixth makes the oldest expire immediately.
- Burgeon: Pyro on a Dendro Core consumes it and causes a larger Dendro explosion, also in a 5 m radius, to enemies and players.
- Hyperbloom: Electro on a Dendro Core turns it into a Sprawling Shot that homes in on the closest enemy and hits for increased Dendro area damage in a 1 m radius. If an enemy or the environment triggers it, it homes on the closest ally instead.
- Damage to players from every Bloom-related reaction is 2% of what the same reaction deals to enemies, whoever triggers it.
- Burgeon and Hyperbloom may be triggered by a different party from the one that made the Core, including the environment, and they scale with the stats of whoever applied the Pyro or Electro.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show Bloom as a bud or seed of green energy that swells out of damp air and then bursts into leaves and spores. Keep the idea of waiting: the Core gives bystanders a moment to move, strike it, or step away.

Examples: A Hydro slime is soaked by a Hydro attack; a Dendro arrow then lands, and a glowing seed forms at its feet. Left alone it bursts in a green shower. If a spark of lightning hits it first, it darts across the field at the nearest enemy.

Limits: Do not claim Bloom can happen without Dendro and Hydro, or that Anemo, Geo or Cryo triggers it. Do not describe Burgeon or Hyperbloom as separate elements; they are second-stage reactions of a Dendro Core.

38.content: A Dendro Core is the bud-like object created by Bloom. It lasts up to 6 seconds and bursts for Dendro area damage within 5 m if the party member who made it is still present and alive. At most 5 can exist at a time. Pyro on it causes Burgeon; Electro on it causes Hyperbloom.

39.content: Burgeon is the reaction that follows when Pyro hits a Dendro Core. It consumes the Core and deals stronger area Dendro damage within 5 m to enemies and players. It can be triggered by a different party, or by the environment, and uses the Pyro applier's stats.

40.content: Hyperbloom is the reaction that follows when Electro hits a Dendro Core. The Core becomes a Sprawling Shot that homes in on the nearest enemy (or ally, if an enemy or the environment triggered it) and deals stronger Dendro area damage in a 1 m radius.

41.content:
Bond of Life (also: Life Bond): Bond of Life is a combat mechanic that prevents healing. Some enemy, weapon or talent effects place it on a character; while it lasts it soaks up incoming healing instead of restoring health. It is a gameplay abstraction, not a story concept.

It was introduced in version 4.0. In the game it appears as a red outline over the character's HP bar.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): while Bond of Life is active, healing the character is absorbed by the bond according to its value rather than restoring HP. It clears once healing equal to its value has been taken in, or when the player visits a Statue of The Seven.

- Maximum value: 200% of the character's Max HP.
- Display: the red outline covers half as much of the HP bar as its value, so a 100% bond overlays 50% of the bar.
- Timeout: if not cleared sooner, it clears 600 seconds (10 minutes) after its last increase.
- After the bond clears, some sources apply additional effects, which depend on whatever applied it.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): portray it as a debt or curse on the body that makes recovery feel useless for a while, with relief at the statue. Do not quote the percentages in character or invent a lore origin for it.

Limits: No in-world account exists; keep it to a combat effect.

Figures above are those listed on the wiki as of 7.1 and may change in later versions.

42.comment: Bond of Life: Bond of Life numbers
42.content: Bond of Life caps at 200% of Max HP, clears after healing equal to its value or after 600 seconds since its last increase, and also clears at a Statue of The Seven.

43.content:
Burgeon (also: Burgeon reaction, Pyro Bloom reaction, Pyro-Dendro Core reaction): Burgeon is a Dendro elemental reaction. A Dendro Core (the seed-like orb a Bloom leaves behind) that is struck by Pyro explodes immediately, in a bigger burst of Dendro damage than the core would deal on its own. It is one of the two ways to cash in a Bloom early, the other being Hyperbloom.

It debuted in Version 3.0 together with Bloom, Hyperbloom, Quicken, Spread and Aggravate, the reactions introduced for Dendro. The reaction cannot happen on its own: a Hydro and Dendro Bloom has to make the core first.

In universe: Canon gives no in-world explanation for Burgeon. The pages read treat it purely as a combat rule, so it is best understood as what fire does to a ripe seed of plant energy.

Gameplay: Gameplay: when Pyro is applied to a Dendro Core, Burgeon triggers. It uses up the core and deals Dendro area damage, wider and heavier than an unaided core burst.

- A Dendro Core normally explodes by itself when its time runs out, but only if the character who made it is still in the party and alive. Burgeon detonates it early, in a 5 m radius.
- The wiki says the damage hits enemies and players alike; damage to players from Bloom-related reactions is 2% of the damage to enemies.
- It can be triggered by a party other than the one that made the Bloom, including the environment, and its damage scales with the party that applied the Pyro.
- Burgeon is a transformative reaction: it does its own damage, based on the triggering character's level and Elemental Mastery, and ignores ATK and cannot critically strike unless a talent or constellation allows it.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show a green, lumpy seed of energy hanging in the air, then a flame touching it and the seed bursting outward in a flare of leaves, sap and heat. Keep it a sudden, loud, fairly local blast.

Limits: Burgeon needs a Dendro Core, so it needs Bloom first. It does nothing to a Bountiful Core.

The explosion can hurt the party too, though far less than it hurts enemies. The core vanishes after its duration if its creator has left the party.

Examples: Gameplay example: Hydro and Dendro together leave a Dendro Core. A Pyro attack on it triggers Burgeon at once and the core blows up in a wide Dendro burst, catching enemies close together.

44.content: A Dendro Core is what the Bloom reaction (Dendro with Hydro) leaves behind. If left alone it bursts after about six seconds. Pyro on it triggers Burgeon, Electro triggers Hyperbloom. No more than five can exist at a time.

45.content:
Burning (also: Burning reaction, Burning aura): Burning is what happens when Pyro and Dendro meet on a target, in either order. It sets the target alight: fire damage over time, a small burst of flame around them, and a flaming aura that lasts while the Dendro on the target lasts. Plants and grass catch fire the same way.

The fire consumes the Dendro as it burns, so it goes out when the plant energy is spent. The wiki lists Burning as a Transformative reaction.

In universe: Canon offers no in-world explanation. Burning appears in tutorials and combat, not in character dialogue in the sources read. Treat it as a gameplay abstraction that a scene may borrow from.

The wiki's Environment section ties it to the open world: Wood objects such as grass, haystacks, shrubs, small trees, crates and barrels burn when Pyro touches them, and a burning creature spreads flame to combustible things it touches.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): applying Pyro to a Dendro-affected target, or Dendro to a Pyro-affected one, triggers Burning. It deals area Pyro damage and applies 1 gauge unit of Pyro within a 1 m radius to players and enemies, with a 2 second internal cooldown on that Pyro application. The Burning aura looks like an animated Pyro aura and coexists with the underlying Pyro and Dendro auras.

- The Dendro aura is steadily consumed during Burning. The state needs both the Burning aura and the Dendro aura, and ends when either runs out.
- Burning cannot damage off-field characters. Switching away pauses the damage ticks but not the Dendro consumption; if the character returns while still affected by Dendro, they resume taking damage.
- For effects that trigger on reactions, such as the Scroll of the Hero of Cinder City artifact set and Nahida's Seeds of Skandha, refreshing a Burning aura with more Pyro or Dendro does not count as triggering Burning again.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show Burning as stubborn fire clinging to something green: leaves curling and blackening, sparks dropping from a smouldering target, grass flaring along the path of a burning enemy. It feeds on the plant energy and dies when that is gone.

Examples: An archer's Dendro arrow sticks to a hilichurl's wooden shield. A fire-slime spark touches it and flames climb the grain, spilling onto the dry grass around it.

Limits: Burning requires both Pyro and Dendro; Anemo, Geo, Hydro, Electro and Cryo do not cause it. Do not describe it as an instant burst; its identity is the continuing burn. A burning character who is switched off the field stops taking Burning damage until they return.

46.content: The Burning aura is the flaming overlay created by the Burning reaction. It coexists with ordinary Pyro and Dendro auras and ends when either the Burning aura or the Dendro aura is used up. Refreshing it with more Pyro or Dendro does not count as another Burning reaction for reaction-triggered effects.

47.content:
Constellation (also: Constellations, Stella Fortuna, star sign, constellation level): "Constellation" means two linked things in Teyvat. In lore, the stars of a constellation stand for a person's fate, and the Heavenly Principles are said to pull those stars like strings on the people of the mortal world. In gameplay, each playable character has six Constellation levels, upgrades unlocked one at a time with that character's Stella Fortuna.

Every Vision holder has a personal star sign: Jean's is Leo Minor, which canon reads as strength and responsibility shouldered too young. The Traveler, Archons, adepti and a few others have special constellations that depict them personally.

In universe: The stars of Teyvat are tied to Fate. Constellations are an extension of that idea: patterns of Stella Fortuna that trace what a person will be, and strings by which the Heavenly Principles direct mortals.

Each Vision holder's fate is linked to a specific constellation, and each constellation represents particular characteristics. Jean's Leo Minor represents "strength and responsibility shouldered too young." People without Visions have fates that are also reflected in the stars, but they do not seem to be tied to named constellations. The stars themselves are physical celestial bodies called Stella Fortuna.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): each playable character (the Traveler is handled separately) has six Constellation levels, unlocked in order by spending one Stella Fortuna per level. Constellation effects work like extra passive talents: they raise effectiveness or add capabilities to existing abilities. The third and fifth levels are normally a three-level boost to one specific Combat Talent.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): characters rarely discuss "Constellation 3" as a number; in-world, a constellation is a star sign and a hint of fate. Use it for atmosphere (a character glancing at the stars, an astrologer reading a pattern) rather than game talk. Mona is the natural voice for this, since she reads fortunes.

48.content: Stella Fortuna are the physical stars that make up a constellation in lore. In gameplay, they are the item that unlocks one Constellation level for the matching character; extra copies at level 6 convert into Masterless Stella Fortuna.

49.content: Constellations are named in Latin-style terms that sometimes match the character: Jean's Leo Minor, Venti's Carmen Dei ("God's Song"), Zhongli's Lapis Dei ("God's Stone"), Albedo's Princeps Cretaceus ("Chalk Prince"), Durin's Draco Rubedo ("Red Dragon") and Xiao's Alatus Nemeseos ("Winged Nemesis"). Columbina is the only character whose constellation name equals her own name.

50.content:
Cryo (also: Cryo element, element of ice, element of frost): Cryo is the element of ice and frost, one of Teyvat's seven elements. Its Archon is Anastasya, the Tsaritsa (divine name Vassaga), God of Love, who rules Snezhnaya, the land of eternal winter. Cryo users chill, freeze and slow their enemies. The Tsaritsa also holds the Cryo Gnosis and, as of 7.1, five of the other six.

Cryo ascension gems are Shivada Jade. The Cryo Dragon Sovereign is long dead, and its corpse is tied to Snezhnaya's ice and crystal ley lines. Cryoculi were added in Snezhnaya in Version 7.0.

In universe: Most people cannot use Cryo. Those who can usually hold a Cryo Vision, a crystal that grants control of the element. The Tsaritsa draws instead on the Cryo Authority of her divine throne in Celestia, and on her Gnosis.

Snezhnaya is the element's home in the world. In the far north is Morepesok, the only port city on the northern coast, known for its birch forests and old forestry industry. In gameplay the Cryo status can coat certain objects as well as creatures, such as ore, Thunderwood and Amber's Baron Bunny, so reactions can occur on them. Frozen is a sibling element carried by enemy ice shields and some Cryo creatures; the Frozen reaction (Cryo with Hydro) holds a target in place.

Archon and nation: Archon: Anastasya Feodorovna Snezhnaya, the Tsaritsa of All Snezhnaya, Cryo Archon of the Seven and God of Love. Her divine name is Vassaga. Nation: Snezhnaya, which she governs directly from Zapolyarny Palace.

She became Cryo Archon about 500 years ago, during the Cataclysm, succeeding the Belyi Tsar after his death on an expedition. Unlike most Archons she runs her nation day to day: her Edicts are the highest authority, and the Fatui, who handle most governance, carry out her will abroad. After the Cataclysm she cut ties with the other Archons, including Venti.

Gnosis and authority: In Ending Note (Prologue, 1.0), Venti explained that a Gnosis is an Archon's internal focus that resonates directly with Celestia, and that the Fatui were gathering them. The Cryo Gnosis is the Tsaritsa's own; her power comes from both it and the Cryo Authority of her Divine Throne.

Elemental beings: Cryo Slimes, Specters, Cicins, Whopperflowers, Regisvines, Abyss Mages and the Cryo Hypostasis are Cryo creatures. The Cryo Dragon Sovereign is dead.

Archive entries describe Cryo Slimes as small monsters formed where Cryo coagulates in nature; in gameplay they freeze the water beneath them, so they cannot drown. Cryo Specters are floating monsters of concentrated Cryo. Cryo Regisvines are vines imbued with biting frost from the ley lines.

Known uses: Chilling and freezing foes, raising ice, and slowing movement.

In Snezhnaya the ice can be broken, shattered and rebuilt to change terrain and enemy movement. Dragonspine's Sheer Cold is an environmental hazard of its climate, separate from the Cryo element.

Limits: Cryo does not react with Dendro.

A Vision fixes its holder to one element. Masterless Visions lose their element and power when their holder dies.

Interactions: Cryo reacts with Electro (Superconduct), Hydro (Frozen), Pyro (Melt), Anemo (Swirl, and Stellar Swirl since 7.0) and Geo (Crystallize). Each has its own entry.

Frozen holds a target in place, and a blunt or Geo hit shatters it. Superconduct lowers Physical resistance. Melt amplifies Cryo hits on Pyro-affected targets. Swirl spreads Cryo to nearby targets, and Crystallize leaves a Cryo shard that gives a shield.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Cryo is a damage type and the element of characters such as Ganyu, Kaeya, Qiqi, Chongyun, Diona, Eula, Rosaria, Shenhe, Kamisato Ayaka, Layla, Wriothesley, Mika, Charlotte, Freminet, Citlali, Escoffier, Skirk and Aloy. The Traveler becomes Cryo by resonating with a Statue of The Seven in Snezhnaya.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show Cryo as stillness, pale blue-white light and falling temperature: breath fogging, frost creeping from a hand, ice that rings or cracks. Keep scale proportionate: a Vision holder can chill a drink, freeze a puddle or raise an ice barrier, but sealing a whole mausoleum in ice is the Archon's work.

51.content: The Cryo Archon is Anastasya Feodorovna Snezhnaya, the Tsaritsa of All Snezhnaya, called the God of Love among the Seven. Her divine name is Vassaga. She succeeded the Belyi Tsar about 500 years ago, rules Snezhnaya from Zapolyarny Palace and appoints the Eleven Fatui Harbingers. She holds the Cryo Gnosis and refuses to use her authority of love.

52.content: The Cryo Dragon was one of the Seven Sovereigns, the dragon-lords who ruled Teyvat before the Heavenly Principles. It fought Celestia and was defeated. Its corpse is the source of Snezhnaya's primordial ice and crystal ley lines.

53.content: Cryoculi are found scattered across Snezhnaya and are offered at Statues of The Seven there. Item text calls the Cryoculus a substance "that has accumulated intense Cryo energy", offered to help a Statue regain power lost over the years. They appeared in 7.0.

54.content:
Crystallize (also: Crystallize reaction, Crystallize shard, Crystallize shield, Elemental Shard): Crystallize is what happens when Geo hits a target already affected by Pyro, Hydro, Electro or Cryo. It deals no damage. It leaves a shard of that element, and a character who picks the shard up gains a shield of the same element.

Geo is always the second element in this reaction. Anemo and Dendro are not part of it.

In universe: Canon offers no in-world explanation. Crystallize shows up in tutorials and combat, not in character dialogue in the sources read. Treat it as a gameplay abstraction that a scene may borrow from.

The in-game tutorial describes it simply: Geo contacting Hydro, Pyro, Cryo or Electro creates shards of the matching element that give the character an elemental shield, and good use of it cuts damage taken in battle.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): the shard (Electro, Pyro, Hydro or Cryo) lasts 15 seconds on the field, with a short delay before it can be picked up. Picking it up grants an elemental shield that also lasts 15 seconds. Enemies cannot pick shards up.

- If more than 3 shards are on the field, after about 2 seconds only the 3 newest remain.
- Only one Crystallize shield is active at a time; a new shard's shield overwrites the old one.
- Crystallize can trigger only once per second on the same target.
- A Geo shard from Geovishap Hatchlings or the Pure Geo Hypostasis is a different thing; its shield can coexist with a Crystallize shield instead of replacing it.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show Crystallize as a coloured stone shard forming in the air around a struck foe: ember-red from fire, blue from water, pale from frost, violet from lightning. Picking it up wraps the character in a pane of matching light.

Examples: A Pyro slime is scorched by a sword, then struck by a Geo strike. A red crystal flies loose, and the character who gathers it is wrapped in a shell of fire-coloured light, which takes less harm from flames.

Limits: Crystallize does not deal damage and does not work with Dendro or Anemo. Enemies cannot pick up the shards.

55.content: A Crystallize shard is the pick-up created by the reaction: Electro, Pyro, Hydro or Cryo according to the element that was crystallised. It can be collected after a short delay and lasts 15 seconds on the field. Only the three newest shards stay if more are produced, and enemies cannot take them.

56.content: The shield granted by a Crystallize shard matches the shard's element and lasts 15 seconds. Its health is based on the Geo user's level and Elemental Mastery. It blocks 2.5 times as much damage from its own element, and only one such shield is active at a time.

57.content:
Delusion (also: Delusions, Evil Eye, Fatui Delusion, counterfeit Vision): Delusions are Vision-like devices made by the Fatui. They let their wielders command an element, can be used by almost anyone, and are said to be far stronger than Visions. The price is the user's vitality: they can drain life force, age the wearer or backfire fatally. How they are made is secret; the evidence points to the remains of dead gods. The Chinese name means "Evil Eye", a counterpart to the "Eye of God".

Few Fatui members outside the Eleven Harbingers hold one, and the Tsaritsa grants them herself, according to the Fatui member Viktor. In practice, Delusions have also been handed to ordinary people in Inazuma and carried by defectors abroad. As of 7.1 the Fatui are working on a finished model that drains only the regenerable part of a user's life force.

In universe: A Delusion looks like a Vision with a Fatui emblem instead of an element symbol. It is a glass orb in a jagged frame, and its colour follows the element it grants. Unlike a Vision, which the gods give to one person, a Delusion can be used by anyone who holds it.

Viktor calls Delusions the pride of the Fatui and says they come by the Tsaritsa's own hand. Pyro Agents, Cicin Mages, Mirror Maidens, Operatives and Oprichniki soldiers are all seen with Delusions in the colour of their element. The Fatui treat the subject as a closely guarded secret, even among themselves.

Origins and production: Canon does not describe a general method. The Delusions made in Inazuma used Crystal Marrow, which holds the Tatarigami curse of the slain god Orobashi. The wiki therefore reads Delusions as made from the remains of gods or other powerful beings, but that inference is not stated as a rule.

Side effects: Delusions drain the user's life force and can backfire. Resistance soldiers in Inazuma aged rapidly; Teppei died of it. Diluc's father Crepus was fatally hurt when one backfired.

Effects vary. In the manga, Diluc carried his father's Delusion for three years without obvious ill effect, and people who already hold a Vision or wield elemental power resist abnormal elemental energy better, according to Emilie. Yelena aged quickly as she used hers to grow the Auguste flowers, and her brother Kirya, using it for the same purpose, aged himself by decades. In the manga, Delusions give off a smell of Mist Grass when used.

Notable users: Harbingers with Delusions in canon: Tartaglia (Electro), Signora (Cryo), Arlecchino (Pyro, used when she draws on her Balemoon Bloodfire) and Pierro (Electro). Others: Fatui Agents, Cicin Mages, Mirror Maidens, Operatives and Oprichniki. Outside the Fatui: Crepus (dead), Diluc (formerly), Yelena (dead), Kirya, and Inazuma's Watatsumi Army soldiers (formerly), among them Teppei (dead).

Gameplay: Gameplay, not lore: Fatui enemies carry Delusions as part of their models. Operative's Constancy, an enhancement material, is dropped by Wind and Frost Operatives and is the item tied to Delusions. In the 7.1 quest, Arlecchino is a temporary trial character who gains Bond of Life quickly during tests, and the player must keep an Abyssal Influence Index from rising too high.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): treat a Delusion as a bargain, not a free power. Show the cost in the user: breathlessness, greying, a look of being older than their years. A Fatui who speaks of one should do so with pride or guarded caution, and never explain how it is made. Let someone who knows Visions sense that a Delusion feels wrong: cold, hungry and without the warm sense of being chosen.

58.content: Diluc's father Crepus used a Delusion to defeat a monster, Ursa the Drake, and it backfired and left him fatally hurt. Diluc's and Kaeya's character stories tell the outcome differently: Diluc's says Crepus died in his arms, Kaeya's says Diluc ended his father's agony. Diluc left the Knights and traced the "counterfeit Visions" to the Fatui; in the manga he also takes up his father's Delusion. In the manga it is a red orb on a glove that raises barbed chains, sometimes wrapped in black fire; this version is manga-only.

59.content: A hidden facility on Yashiori Island, found by the Traveler during the Inazuma Archon Quest (2.1). Fatui staff made Delusions there from Crystal Marrow, supplied via the Kanjou Commission. The Balladeer said the Fatui gained from the Vision Hunt Decree because it created demand. The Resistance destroyed the factory. Kokomi had already ordered the army to stop using Delusions after soldiers began to age.

60.content: Resistance soldiers, ambitious people opposed to the Vision Hunt Decree, secretly used Fatui Delusions and began to age fast. Gorou seized one, a black orb with a pale grey Fatui emblem, and showed it to the Traveler. Teppei, a soldier who never owned a Vision, had used one and was dying of its effects. Kokomi ordered the army to stop using them.

61.content:
Dendro (also: Dendro element, element of plants, element of grass): Dendro is the element of plants and growth, one of Teyvat's seven elements. Its Archon is the God of Wisdom, whose divine name is Buer and who today is Lesser Lord Kusanali (Nahida); her nation is Sumeru, a land of rainforest and desert. Dendro Visions let their holders call up vines, leaves and seeds, and it is the element behind Quicken and Bloom reactions. The Dendro Dragon Sovereign is Apep, who once ruled all of Sumeru. Nahida traded her Dendro Gnosis to the Harbinger Dottore in Chapter III, and as of 7.1 the Tsaritsa holds six Gnoses.

Dendro ascension gems are Nagadus Emeralds. Dendro was the last element to gain a playable character, arriving only in Version 3.0 with Tighnari and Collei and the Dendro-aligned Traveler. The Traveler's resonance with Dendro is remarked on by several characters in Chapter III.

In universe: Most people can only use Dendro through a Dendro Vision; Nahida draws on the Dendro Authority of her divine throne in Celestia. In Sumeru, Dendro is bound up with life, growth and dreams: the rainforest, its Aranara, and the Akasha network all trace back to the God of Wisdom.

Greater Lord Rukkhadevata, the first Dendro Archon, is credited with reviving the rainforest from desert, creating the Aranara, and guiding the people who founded the Sumeru Akademiya. Dendro is also the element of her "wisdom": the Akasha System she created used the Dendro Gnosis to link minds. Nahida, her successor, is hardly a fighter; her power is chiefly over dreams, consciousness and plants.

Archon and nation: Archon: the God of Wisdom, divine name Buer. The current holder is Lesser Lord Kusanali (Nahida); before her it was Greater Lord Rukkhadevata. Nation: Sumeru, whose capital Sumeru City is built on the Divine Tree.

Rukkhadevata perished in the cataclysm about 500 years ago. Before dying she created Kusanali as her next incarnation, but she had exhausted herself fighting the Abyss, so Kusanali was born as a child with no memories. In Chapter III's finale (Where the Boat of Consciousness Lies), Nahida removed all memory of Rukkhadevata from Irminsul at Rukkhadevata's own request, to eradicate forbidden knowledge from the world. As a result everyone, Nahida included, now believes Kusanali has always been the sole Dendro Archon; only the Traveler remembers the truth.

Gnosis and authority: Dendro's Gnosis belonged first to Rukkhadevata and powered the Akasha System, then to Nahida. In Chapter III Nahida gave Dottore the Dendro Gnosis in exchange for knowledge about the false sky. She also took the Electro Gnosis from Scaramouche's fallen "Shouki no Kami" and later gave it to Dottore in exchange for his agreeing to erase his Segments. A Gnosis is not required for an Archon to hold their power: Nahida stays the Dendro Archon with no Dendro Gnosis.

Elemental beings: Apep, the Dendro Dragon Sovereign, and Dendro elemental lifeforms such as slimes, specters and the Dendro Hypostasis.

Apep survived the old world's wars and is still alive; the Traveler and Nahida helped her in the 3.6 quest Homecoming. Dendro Samachurls are hilichurl shamans who attack with vines and poison; Dendro Slimes are slimes shaped by abundant Dendro in their environment, which also gives them Dendro's weaknesses.

Known uses: Vines, leaves, seeds and plants grown or controlled, and Dendro Cores from Bloom. Some Dendro enemies, such as Large Dendro Slimes, inflict a poison status.

Nahida's power over dreams and consciousness is part of her Dendro Authority. Tighnari and Collei, Sumeru's rainforest rangers, hold Dendro Visions. The Sumeru rainforest itself is Rukkhadevata's work.

Limits: Dendro does not react with Anemo or Geo.

Dendro reacts with Hydro, Electro and Pyro only. A Vision fixes its bearer to one element.

Interactions: Quicken (Dendro + Electro) leads to Aggravate and Spread. Bloom (Dendro + Hydro) creates a Dendro Core, which can become Hyperbloom with Electro or Burgeon with Pyro. Burning (Dendro + Pyro) ignites. Each is its own entry.

Lunar-Bloom (6.0) is a Lunar reaction version of Bloom: with certain characters in the party, Bloom becomes Lunar-Bloom and grants the party Verdant Dew.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Dendro is a damage type and the element of Nahida, Tighnari, Collei, Baizhu, Alhaitham, Kaveh, Yaoyao, Kirara, Emilie, Lauma, Nefer and others. The Traveler can switch to Dendro after resonating with a Statue of The Seven in Sumeru.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show Dendro as growth, scent and gentle light: leaves unfurling, vines tightening, fresh-cut grass, green glow with golden accents. Keep scale proportionate: a Vision holder can summon vines and seeds, not raise a forest. Dream-shaping and consciousness are Nahida's Authority, not general Dendro skills.

62.content: The Dendro Archon is the God of Wisdom, protector of Sumeru. There have been two holders: Greater Lord Rukkhadevata, who died in the cataclysm about 500 years ago, and her reincarnation Lesser Lord Kusanali (Nahida). In Chapter III Nahida erased Rukkhadevata from Irminsul, so the world remembers only Kusanali.

63.content: A Dendroculus is an Adventure Item scattered across Sumeru; item text calls it a substance "that has accumulated intense Dendro energy" which can be offered to a Statue of The Seven to restore power it has lost.

64.content: Nagadus Emeralds are the ascension gems used for Dendro characters.

65.content:
Diving (also: underwater exploration, Transoceanic Sourcewater, Fontaine's Blessing, Aquatic Stamina): Diving is how the Traveler explores underwater in Fontaine. Fontaine's lakes can be dived in once the first Statue of The Seven there is activated; a power called the Transoceanic Sourcewater keeps Vision holders, the Traveler and Paimon from drowning and lets them breathe and speak underwater. Ordinary people without Visions need diving gear and training. Fontaine is the only nation where diving is a game mechanic.

Diving is a recognised profession in Fontaine, and a diving certificate can be earned there, according to Vasco. It arrived in Version 4.0 with Fontaine.

In universe: The tutorial calls the power the "Transoceanic Sourcewater" and says it flows out from a Statue of The Seven to bless those moving through Fontaine's lakes. In the text of the world, it lets Vision holders (and certain others, such as the Traveler and Paimon) breathe and speak underwater.

People without Visions rely on diving gear and must complete specialised training. The diver Archenoul, hired by Spina di Rosula, says such newcomers must first go down with a professional, and warns that cramps or ringing in the ears can follow if a diver skips a warm-up or fails to adapt to water pressure. The Traveler also dives comfortably in the Sea of Bygone Eras, said to lie beneath depths untouched by sunlight, so cold and darkness do not seem to trouble them either.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Diving unlocks after activating the first Statue of The Seven in Fontaine, once the quest The Outlander Who Caught the Wind is complete. While diving the party cannot drown and uses Aquatic Stamina for fast swimming instead of ordinary Stamina; Aquatic Stamina cannot be increased or unlocked further. Characters share the same underwater abilities and can still be switched. Diving works in the lakes of the raised mainland and the Sea of Bygone Eras, but not in the lower surrounding waters or around the Nostoi region (the sea around Petrichor, per the Fontaine page).

Limits: Diving is a Fontaine mechanic and does not apply in other nations.

Ordinary Swimming outside Fontaine uses Stamina, and the party cannot fight while swimming. Non-Vision holders in the story cannot dive freely without gear and training.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): treat the Sourcewater as a quiet, protective blessing. Vision holders, the Traveler and Paimon can talk and breathe underwater as if in air, while ordinary NPCs wear divesuits and take pre-dive precautions. Do not let an ordinary Fontainian simply dive without gear.

66.content: The Transoceanic Sourcewater is the power behind diving in Fontaine. Tutorial text says it flows from a Statue of The Seven, protects those moving through the lakes and lets them breathe and speak underwater if they hold a Vision (and for the Traveler and Paimon). Its origin is not explained.
