How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): present Lunar-Bloom as the same seed-like burst as Bloom with an added pale shine, and Verdant Dew as small drops that gather and are spent. Keep it tied to a team that includes a Moonsign Benediction user.

Limits: Lunar-Bloom does not deal damage when it triggers; the dew must be spent by a character that can use it.

Dew caps at 3. Dendro Core and Bountiful Core damage is not Lunar-Bloom damage.

135.content: Verdant Dew is the resource Lunar-Bloom grants: 1 every 2.5 seconds for 2.5 seconds after the reaction, up to 3, never expiring. Certain characters consume it to deal Lunar-Bloom damage to enemies.

136.content:
Lunar-Charged (also: Lunar Charged, Lunar-Charged reaction, thundercloud reaction): Lunar-Charged is the Lunar Reaction between Electro and Hydro. When the two meet on a target and the party includes a character whose Moonsign Benediction passive enables it, the usual Electro-Charged is replaced by Lunar-Charged. The reaction forms a thundercloud that keeps firing lightning at nearby enemies carrying both Electro and Hydro. Its damage can crit. It was the first Lunar Reaction, arriving in Version 5.8 alongside Ineffa.

Unlike Electro-Charged, the damage is based on every character who applied an element during the reaction, so the whole party shares in it. The damage is Electro.

In universe: Canon offers no in-world explanation. The thundercloud is shown only in tutorial and combat material. Treat it as a gameplay abstraction that a scene may borrow as a storm gathering over a fight.

Related setting: Ineffa, the character who introduced the reaction, is a 5-star Electro polearm user, and the reaction came out in 5.8, before the Nod-Krai region opened in 6.0. The wiki also lists a Genius Invokation TCG summon called Thundercloud created by Lunar-Charged; that is a card game effect, not a story event.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): the thundercloud deals Electro damage to all Wet enemies who are also affected by Electro within roughly 5 m, every 2 seconds. A target that has not been hit in the last 2 seconds and is Wet or Electro-affected is struck at once when the other aura lands on it.

- Each strike uses up 0.4 gauge units of the Wet and Electro auras together.
- The cloud lasts 6 seconds, which resets if another Lunar-Charged triggers. Only one cloud exists at a time; triggering outside its range makes a new one and removes the old one.
- Thunderclouds try to position themselves between active targets and the triggering party.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show a small, low thundercloud that follows the fight, flickers when Electro and water are on the same enemy, and drops short bolts. Keep it a visible, compact storm rather than a weather event. Reserve it for scenes with an Electro user and a Hydro user.

Limits: The cloud only strikes enemies that carry both Electro and Hydro (Wet), and only one cloud can exist at a time.

Without a Moonsign Benediction character who enables it, Electro meeting Hydro simply makes the ordinary Electro-Charged.

137.content: A thundercloud is the object created by a Lunar-Charged reaction. It lasts 6 seconds, drifts between targets and the triggering party, and fires Electro damage at nearby enemies that are both Wet and affected by Electro. A Genius Invokation TCG summon shares the name.

138.content:
Lunar-Crystallize (also: Lunar Crystallize, Lunar-Crystallize reaction, Moondrift Harmony): Lunar-Crystallize is the Lunar Reaction between Geo and Hydro. When the party includes a character whose Moonsign Benediction passive enables it, Hydro Crystallize is replaced by Lunar-Crystallize, which creates three Moondrifts around the target. Every third Lunar-Crystallize while Moondrifts are present sets them resonating in Moondrift Harmony, a tracking projectile that deals Geo damage and can crit. It arrived in Version 6.3 (Luna IV).

As with the other Lunar Reactions, the damage is based on every character who applied an element during the reaction, and it can also be dealt directly by a talent. The wiki treats Moondrifts as Geo constructs.

In universe: Canon offers no in-world explanation. Moondrifts and Moondrift Harmony appear in tutorial and combat material only. Treat them as a gameplay abstraction.

Related setting: the reaction came to the Nod-Krai-themed Moonsign family later than Lunar-Charged and Lunar-Bloom. The wiki's announcement images for it describe it as Hydro and Geo meeting again under the moonlight; that wording is the announcement's, not a statement about the story world.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): triggering Lunar-Crystallize makes three Moondrifts near the target. While at least one is on the field, each third Lunar-Crystallize makes them resonate and fire a projectile that tracks the target for Geo damage.

- The wiki classes Moondrifts as Geo constructs.
- The tutorial says triggering the reaction three times starts Moondrift Harmony, which hits nearby opponents with Geo damage.
- Damage can crit and is shared across contributing characters who applied Geo or Hydro.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show three small floating stones circling a foe that glow pale and then fly together in a single strike. Keep them small; they are summoned by a reaction, not a landslide.

Limits: Without a Moonsign Benediction character who enables it, Geo meeting Hydro is ordinary Hydro Crystallize.

Moondrift Harmony needs Moondrifts on the field and fires only on every third Lunar-Crystallize.

139.content: A Moondrift is one of three objects a Lunar-Crystallize creates near the target. While they are on the field, every third Lunar-Crystallize makes them resonate in Moondrift Harmony, firing a Geo projectile that tracks the target. They count as Geo constructs.

140.content:
Lunar Reaction (also: Lunar Reactions, Lunar reaction family, Moonlight Reaction): Lunar Reactions are a family of three elemental reactions that appear when a party contains a character whose Moonsign Benediction passive allows them. Each one takes a normal Hydro-related reaction (Electro-Charged, Bloom, Crystallize) and replaces it with a Moon-themed version: Lunar-Charged, Lunar-Bloom and Lunar-Crystallize. Unlike their base versions, Lunar Reactions can land critical hits. They belong to the Nod-Krai era of the game.

They arrived in stages: Lunar-Charged in Version 5.8, Lunar-Bloom in Version 6.0 (Luna I) and Lunar-Crystallize in Version 6.3 (Luna IV). Lunar-Charged and Lunar-Crystallize can be set off by simply applying the right elements; Lunar-Bloom does no damage by itself and works through character talents and constellations.

In universe: Canon offers no in-world explanation. Lunar Reactions are presented as tutorial and combat material. Treat them as a gameplay abstraction: a scene may borrow the look (moonlit clouds, drifting stones, glowing dew) without naming an in-world law.

Related setting, from the wiki: the reactions are tied to Moonsign, a party bonus keyed to characters of Nod-Krai (plus Zibai), and their enabling passives are called Moonsign Benedictions. Columbina, the new Moon Goddess in the wiki's account, and users of the Moon Wheel are the ones whose passives turn the reactions on. Nod-Krai is also where kuuvahki, described as the power of the Three Moons, is found.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): while a character with a matching Moonsign Benediction is in the party, three Hydro-related reactions are replaced. Electro and Hydro give Lunar-Charged instead of Electro-Charged; Dendro and Hydro give Lunar-Bloom instead of Bloom; Geo and Hydro give Lunar-Crystallize instead of Hydro Crystallize.

- Lunar Reactions can land critical hits, which their base versions cannot.
- Lunar-Charged makes a thundercloud, Lunar-Bloom gives Verdant Dew, and Lunar-Crystallize makes Moondrifts (each has its own entry).
- Lunar-Charged and Lunar-Crystallize can deal damage through a separate instance when elements are applied, using the stats of every character that contributed an element. Lunar-Bloom damage comes only from talents and constellations.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): give Lunar Reactions a cool, silvery cast. A thundercloud drifting between fighters, a ring of floating stones, dew beading on leaves under moonlight. Keep them tied to someone with a Moonsign Benediction, since that is what the game requires.

Limits: Without a Moonsign Benediction character in the party, nothing changes and the ordinary reactions occur.

Lunar-Bloom does not make its own damage when it triggers; the Dendro Cores it creates are ordinary Bloom cores and do not count as Lunar-Bloom damage.

141.content: The three Lunar Reactions are Lunar-Charged (Electro with Hydro, replaces Electro-Charged, 5.8), Lunar-Bloom (Dendro with Hydro, replaces Bloom, 6.0) and Lunar-Crystallize (Geo with Hydro, replaces Hydro Crystallize, 6.3). Each has a matching entry for its details.

142.content:
Melt (also: Melt reaction, Melt DMG, Pyro-Cryo reaction): Melt is the elemental reaction between Pyro and Cryo. It deals no damage itself. Instead, the attack that triggers it hits harder. The bonus is larger when the trigger is Pyro landing on a target already affected by Cryo, and smaller when Cryo lands on a Pyro-affected target. It is a combat rule, so treat it as a gameplay abstraction, not a named law of the world.

Melt has existed since Version 1.0. Its sibling amplifying reaction is Vaporize (Pyro with Hydro). Both give damage multipliers, and neither creates a new effect on the target.

In universe: Canon gives no story explanation for Melt. The in-game tutorial only says that when Pyro meets Cryo, Melt occurs, and the triggering source of damage receives a bonus.

Nothing read ties Melt to a character or event. Do not invent an origin. The everyday idea that heat melts ice is a safe image for a scene, but treat it as flavour.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Melt happens when Pyro hits a target that already carries Cryo, or when Cryo hits a target that already carries Pyro. The triggering attack's damage is multiplied. Pyro as the trigger gives a 2x multiplier; Cryo as the trigger gives 1.5x.

- Elemental Mastery of the triggering character raises the multiplier further, and certain artifact sets raise Melt damage.
- The 2x version consumes more of the first element, usually removing it quickly. The 1.5x version consumes less and often leaves the aura in place.
- Applying Pyro to a Freeze Aura left by Frozen consumes it and triggers Melt. Melt can also dissolve ice on water in the open world instantly.

Limits: Melt cannot happen without a first element in place, and it does nothing to a target with neither Pyro nor Cryo on it.

It adds no damage of its own, so a weak hit stays weak. Enemies immune or resistant to Pyro or Cryo reduce the benefit.

Examples: Gameplay example from the in-game tutorial: use Cryo attacks to coat opponents with Cryo, then switch to a Pyro character and attack; the Pyro attack triggers Melt and hits much harder, so opponents fall faster. The wiki's preview shows Melt being caused on a Cryo Slime.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show Melt as a burst of steam and a hiss where flame meets frost, with the strike landing harder than it should. Pyro is the orange-red cue, Cryo the pale-blue cue; keep the effect to one blow, not a lasting area of fire or ice.

143.content:
Moon Wheel (also: Moon Wheels, Nod-Krai Vision): A Moon Wheel is a Vision-like gem associated with Nod-Krai and the Three Moons. It is "formed from the stuff of the soul" and lets its bearer manipulate the elements like a Vision does, but it draws on kuuvahki, an ancient and purer form of elemental power, instead of ordinary elemental energy. In Nod-Krai a Moon Wheel looks identical to a Vision.

All playable Moon Wheel users hold a Moonsign Benediction passive, the talent that links them to the Moonsign mechanic and to Lunar Reactions (own entries). The known users are Ineffa, Flins, Lauma, Linnea, Nefer and Zibai.

In universe: Moon Wheels work like Visions in practice: the bearer wears the gem and channels one element. The difference is the energy behind it. Kuuvahki is described as a primordial form of elemental power, the power of the Three Moons.

The wiki's lore summary is that the Heavenly Principles and the Three Moon Sisters originally created Moon Wheels, and that they were given to the Moon Goddesses' human followers so the Goddesses could talk with them during rituals. A Natlan-era note in Ineffa's story calls the Moon Wheel a plaything the "traitors" (the Three Moons) gave their human followers to communicate with, and says it relies on a purer power rather than on elemental energy "tainted" by the usurper, the Heavenly Principles.

Appearance: A Nod-Krai Moon Wheel is an orb-shaped elemental gem set in the upper part of a circular frame, with a crescent-like small circle and four rhombuses on the lower half. It is visually identical to a Nod-Krai Vision.

Origins: Item text from the Aubade of Morningstar and Moon artifact set tells of an age of three moons when people, frightened by questions the gods' envoys would not answer, turned to the Three Moons, who answered with madness and inspiration beneath the moon. An archpriestess then returned from a mountain summit with a small circular talisman, called the "Moon Wheel", the new pact between the three moons and the people.

Users: Playable Moon Wheel users: Ineffa (Electro), Flins (Electro), Lauma (Dendro), Linnea (Geo), Nefer (Dendro) and Zibai (Geo). Sigurd's Electro gem might also be a Moon Wheel; this is unknown.

Kuuvahki link: Kuuvahki is found only in Nod-Krai and is described as the power of the Light Realm in its purest form. Lunar Reactions use kuuvahki, and Moon Wheel users enable them through their Moonsign Benediction passives.

Gameplay: Gameplay, not literal lore: Moon Wheel users are playable characters from Nod-Krai (plus Zibai) who carry a Moonsign Benediction passive. Each passive raises the party's Moonsign level by 1, and Moon Wheel users enable and strengthen Lunar Reactions.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): treat a Moon Wheel in a scene like a Vision, a gem at the hip or back that glows with its element. Pale, silvery light is a safe cue for kuuvahki.

Limits: Canon does not say who can receive a Moon Wheel, whether it needs a particular wish or desire (as Visions are said to), or whether a Moon Wheel and a Vision can be held together. It does not say an ordinary person can buy one.

144.comment: Moon Wheel: Moon Wheel and Vision
144.content: Moon Wheels look the same as Nod-Krai Visions, but are "formed from the stuff of the soul" and use kuuvahki rather than normal elemental energy. They were originally given to the Moon Goddesses' followers to let the Goddesses speak with them.

145.content:
Moonsign (also: Moonsign Level, Nascent Gleam, Ascendant Gleam, Moonsign: Nascent Gleam, Moonsign: Ascendant Gleam, New Moon's Embrace): Moonsign is a Team Bonus that sits beside Elemental Resonance. Some characters, mostly from Nod-Krai, carry a Moonsign Benediction passive, and each one in the party raises the party's Moonsign Level by one. One Moonsign character gives Nascent Gleam; two or more give Ascendant Gleam, which strengthens those characters and rewards non-Moonsign teammates for their skills. It is a game system, not a thing characters talk about, and it is tied to the moon-themed power of Nod-Krai.

It first appeared in Version Luna I (6.0), the first Nod-Krai version. The Lunar Reactions it supports (Lunar-Charged from 5.8, Lunar-Bloom from 6.0, Lunar-Crystallize later) are separate systems.

In universe: Canon never explains Moonsign inside the story. The only in-world frame is the one the game gives: Nod-Krai is where "the new moon rises", and the tutorial says there are other ways to raise a party's Moonsign Level there.

The related lore is concrete, though. Moon Wheels are Vision-like gems that channel kuuvahki, the moon-linked primordial elemental power found in Nod-Krai, and every playable Moon Wheel user has a Moonsign Benediction passive. Kuuvahki is described as the power of the Three Moons, spread over Nod-Krai by the new Moon Goddess Columbina. Moonsign should be read as the game's way of showing a team gathering around that moonlight; canon does not describe it as an in-world ritual or ranking.

Mechanics: Gameplay (not literal lore): the party gets a Moonsign Level equal to the number of Moonsign characters in it. One gives the Nascent Gleam effect. Two or more give Ascendant Gleam, which also includes Nascent Gleam's effects.

At Ascendant Gleam, certain Talents and Skills of the Moonsign characters themselves are enhanced. In addition, for 20 seconds after a non-Moonsign character uses an Elemental Skill or Elemental Burst, nearby characters deal more Lunar Reaction DMG, up to 36% and not stacking. How much depends on the caster's element: for Pyro, Electro and Cryo, 0.9% per 100 ATK; for Hydro, 0.6% per 1,000 Max HP; for Geo, 1% per 100 DEF; for Anemo and Dendro, 2.25% per 100 Elemental Mastery.

Moonsign benediction: A Moonsign Benediction passive is the Talent that adds one Moonsign Level while its owner is in the party. Gameplay: the passives are Ineffa's Assemblage Hub, Flins's Old World Secrets, Lauma's Nature's Chorus, Aino's Force Limit Analysis, Nefer's Dusklit Eaves, Jahoda's Rooftop Dash, Columbina's Moonlight, Lent Unto You, Illuga's Unwithering in Winter, Zibai's The Coursing Sun and Moon and Linnea's Habitat Survey.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): Moonsign is a gameplay label and ordinary characters should not mention Moonsign Levels, "Nascent Gleam" or "Ascendant Gleam". If a scene wants the flavour, use soft silver or pale light, quiet confidence and a sense of people drawing strength from one another near Nod-Krai's moonlight, without claiming characters can feel a numbered level.

146.content: Nascent Gleam is the Moonsign effect for a party with one Moonsign character; every party member gains it. It is the lower of the two named levels. Ascendant Gleam includes Nascent Gleam's effects.

147.content: Ascendant Gleam is the Moonsign effect for a party with two or more Moonsign characters. It enhances Moonsign characters' Talents and Skills and lets non-Moonsign characters boost nearby Lunar Reaction DMG for 20 seconds after using a skill or burst, up to a 36% cap. In Genius Invokation TCG, "Moonsign: Ascendant Gleam" is also an Elemental Resonance event card, with the in-card line "Come night or day, may the moonlight connect us."

148.content: The Talent type that adds a Moonsign Level. Characters who have one: Ineffa, Flins, Lauma, Aino, Nefer, Jahoda, Columbina, Illuga, Zibai and Linnea. Passives of Columbina and the Moon Wheel users also enable Lunar Reactions.

149.content:
Moonsign Benediction Passive (also: Moonsign Benediction, Moonsign Benediction Passives, Benediction passive): A Moonsign Benediction passive is a Passive Talent carried by certain characters, mostly from Nod-Krai plus Zibai of Liyue. While its owner is in the party, the party's Moonsign Level rises by one. On Columbina and on Moon Wheel users, the passive also lets a base reaction turn into a Lunar Reaction. It is a game-mechanic label, not something characters discuss in the story.

Official wiki phrasing ties the passive to the Moonsign Team Bonus, which sits beside Elemental Resonance: one Moonsign character gives Nascent Gleam, two or more give Ascendant Gleam.

Gameplay: Game mechanics, not lore. Every Benediction passive adds +1 Moonsign Level while its owner is in the party. Illuga, Jahoda and Aino have only this plain form.

The Lunar-enabling passives convert a base reaction triggered by any party member and add Base DMG that scales with a stat of the owner, per the wiki. Ineffa and Flins convert Electro-Charged into Lunar-Charged (0.7% Base DMG per 100 ATK, up to 14%). Lauma and Nefer convert Bloom into Lunar-Bloom (0.0175% per point of Elemental Mastery, up to 14%). Zibai and Linnea convert Hydro Crystallize into Lunar-Crystallize (0.7% per 100 DEF, up to 14%). Columbina converts all three (Electro-Charged, Bloom and Hydro Crystallize) into their Lunar forms, adding 0.2% Base DMG per 1,000 Max HP, up to 7%.

Roster: Passive, owner and release as listed by the wiki:
- Assemblage Hub: Ineffa (5.8), Electro-Charged to Lunar-Charged.
- Old World Secrets: Flins (Luna I, 6.0), Electro-Charged to Lunar-Charged.
- Nature's Chorus: Lauma (Luna I, 6.0), Bloom to Lunar-Bloom.
- Force Limit Analysis: Aino (Luna I, 6.0), Moonsign level only.
- Dusklit Eaves: Nefer (Luna II, 6.1), Bloom to Lunar-Bloom.
- Rooftop Dash: Jahoda (Luna III, 6.2), Moonsign level only.
- Moonlight, Lent Unto You: Columbina (Luna IV, 6.3), all three conversions.
- The Coursing Sun and Moon: Zibai (Luna IV, 6.3), Hydro Crystallize to Lunar-Crystallize.
- Unwithering in Winter: Illuga (Luna IV, 6.3), Moonsign level only.
- Habitat Survey: Linnea (Luna VI, 6.5), Hydro Crystallize to Lunar-Crystallize.

In universe: Nothing found presents the Benediction as an in-world ritual. The surrounding themes come from Nod-Krai lore: kuuvahki, the moon-linked primordial energy, the Moon Wheels that channel it, and the Moon Goddess Columbina. Treat the passive as the game's way of showing a team gathering under that moonlight, not as a title or rank.

How {{char}} behaves: Project-recommended narrative interpretation, not canon. Characters should not say "my Moonsign Benediction passive" or quote numbers. If a scene needs the idea, show moonlight making a shared effort stronger: the owner steadies the party's reactions, and other teammates feed it through their own skills.

Limits: Do not state that Zibai or any non-Nod-Krai character is a Nod-Krai native because they carry the passive. Do not claim a Moonsign rank exists in society. Do not assume Illuga, Jahoda or Aino alter reactions. Co-Op behaviour of Moonsign is unverified.

150.comment: Moonsign Benediction Passive: Moonsign Benediction passives
150.content: The Talent type that adds one Moonsign Level while its owner is in the party. Owners: Ineffa, Flins, Lauma, Aino, Nefer, Jahoda, Columbina, Illuga, Zibai and Linnea. The passives of Columbina and the Moon Wheel users also enable Lunar Reactions.

151.content:
Mystic Arts in Teyvat (also: Mystic Arts, mystic arts of Teyvat, magic in Teyvat): "Mystic arts" is the wiki's umbrella for the magical, ritual and supernatural traditions of Teyvat that are not just a Vision's elemental power. Mondstadt has openly practised alchemy and astrology; Liyue has the adepti's arts, exorcism, the Art of Homa and the Qimen arts; Inazuma has kitsune and bake-danuki magic, onmyoudou and tengu arts; Sumeru has the Akasha, Akademiya alchemy and the Aranara's Ararakalari. A parallel circle of powerful mages, the Hexenzirkel, practises witchcraft (its own entry).

The grouping is the wiki's, not the game's: each tradition keeps its own in-world name and rules. The mystic arts are mostly shown by what particular people can do, not by a rulebook; canon explains very little about how any of it works. Nation entries and the Alchemy, Art of Khemia, Adeptal Arts, Exorcism and Witchcraft entries carry the detail.

In universe: Magic is not limited to Vision-bearers: Yelan says her clan has practised it for generations, and kitsune, adepti, tengu and aranara work wonders without Visions. Arts include divination, talismans, transformation, dream-magic, pocket dimensions, purification, alchemy and spirit-summoning.

Many traditions inherit from each other. The adepti's arts were taught to them by Rex Lapis. Liyue's exorcist arts look like derivatives of adeptal arts. Inazuma's onmyoudou was built by Kamuna Harunosuke 500 years ago from adeptal techniques and the tengu art of transcension. The Fantastic Compass, invented by the adeptus Sea Gazer, was handed to a mortal exorcist friend and later reached Yelan's family, which developed its own catalysts.

Mondstadt: Alchemy is openly practised (bio-alchemy and Albedo's Art of Khemia). Astrology, including hydromancy, is practised by Barbeloth and Mona.

Liyue: The adepti's Adeptus Arts, taught to them by Rex Lapis (adeptal alchemy, dream-magic, talismans, pocket dimensions), plus exorcism, the Art of Homa and the Qimen arts.

Inazuma: Inazuma has the kitsune and bake-danuki's shapeshifting magic (Yae Miko is a master of kitsune spells), onmyoudou (paper shikigami and shikifuda, largely lost) and the tengu's feather-fan arts.

Sumeru: Sumeru has the Akasha knowledge system, Akademiya alchemy and the Aranara's memory-powered Ararakalari.

Other regions: The wiki page covers only Mondstadt, Liyue, Inazuma and Sumeru. Other nations have their own non-Vision traditions that live in separate entries: Natlan's Nightsoul, Nod-Krai's Moonsign and Moonchanters, and Khaenri'ah's Khemia. Fontaine's mystic traditions are not covered by the wiki page.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): treat each tradition as belonging to a place, a lineage and a way of thinking, not as a generic spell list. Liyue's arts are talismans, formulas and discipline; Inazuma's are paper charms and transformations; Sumeru's are knowledge, memory and lectures; Mondstadt's are lab benches and star charts. Magic should cost something: focus, memory, health, a rare tool or a partner.

Limits: Canon never defines a unified magic system. Arts are tied to teachers and lineages and some are lost (most onmyoudou; kitsune power after the Saiguu). Some carry serious risks: adeptal elixirs kill non-adepti, the Nuo Dance inflicts great suffering, Homa can shorten a life, and astrologers risk entangling their own fate.

152.comment: Mystic Arts in Teyvat: Astrology and Hydromancy
152.content: Astrology infers fate from the movements of stars. Barbeloth and her student Mona practise it; hydromancy is the subclass in which the starlight's inverted reflection on water is read. Mona says reading your own fate makes it turn in on itself and advising a subject can entangle your fates. The Traveler's fate cannot be read this way. Pyromancy is a presumed fire divination known only from a single note.

153.comment: Mystic Arts in Teyvat: Adeptus Arts
153.content: The adepti's arts were taught to them by Rex Lapis. Besides controlling the elements, adepti can make elixirs, give or receive dreams, remain in human form after death, use yaksha masks, store power in talismans, and create pocket dimensions with teapot-spirit servants. See the Adeptal Arts entry.

154.comment: Mystic Arts in Teyvat: Art of Homa
154.content: A secret technique of the Wangsheng Funeral Parlor that purifies fetor, the leakage of death into the world of the living. Hu Tao says it needs great focus and no hesitation; mistakes can shorten the practitioner's life. Wuwang Kid passed it to the Parlor's founders after the Lone Butterfly of the Crimson Flame's death.

155.comment: Mystic Arts in Teyvat: Qimen Arts
155.content: A set of Liyue techniques including fortune-telling, fate transference, illusion-making and warding off evil, originated by the Wind Reader of the Eight Adepts. The Lan Clan of Chenyu Vale uses them for both duty and craft; one form uses rattan figures. Lan Junming also taught a Soul-Binding Art that was later outlawed.

156.content: Liyue's exorcists (thaumaturges) swear to cleanse the land of ghosts, spirits and demons and are skilled in combat, magic and martial arts. Most come from families that hold the trade, among them the Tianheng Thaumaturges (Chongyun, and Shenhe's mother), Yelan's clan and the Lan Clan. Their arts seem derived from adeptal arts; every exorcist seen using them in-game has a Vision. See the Exorcism entry.

157.content: Inazuma's Kamuna art of paper-based charm magic, created by Kamuna Harunosuke 500 years ago from adeptal techniques and the tengu art of transcension. Shikigami are enchanted paper cut-outs; shikifuda are elemental seals. It is largely lost, though the Kairagi use shikifuda, and its techniques survive in devices like the Ubiquity Nets and the Mystic Onmyou Chamber.

158.content: The Aranara's memory-fuelled abilities. Each Aranara has a unique power that can attack, teleport or shield against the Withering, spends their memories when used, and can grow with new memories. A Kusava seed amplifies it and lets humans use it briefly.

159.comment: Mystic Arts in Teyvat: Akasha System
159.content: Sumeru's Gnosis-powered knowledge network, created by Greater Lord Rukkhadevata and developed by the Akademiya. A terminal gives its user any knowledge they seek; Lesser Lord Kusanali calls herself the first Akasha Terminal. Terminals can also work without the Akasha, from stored Canned Knowledge in Knowledge Capsules.

160.content:
Nightsoul's Blessing (also: Nightsouls, Nightsoul Burst, Nightsoul Transmission, Nightsoul Points, Nightsoul-aligned): Nightsoul's Blessing is the power state of Natlan's warriors. Natlan's dead enter the Night Kingdom, a realm of souls beneath the land; the souls there are called Nightsouls, and Natlanese fighters borrow their strength to run, climb, swim, leap and fight beyond what they could alone. The Wayob, spirits venerated by the six tribes, live in that realm, which the Lord of the Night made. It is a Natlan power tied to the land's own rules, not an element.

In play, the state is entered mostly through a character's Elemental Skill, runs on a pool of Nightsoul points, and is stronger inside Natlan. It is separate from the Vision system, though many Natlanese fighters use both.

In universe: In story terms, the Night Kingdom is "a liminal space between the body and mind, life and death," deep underground. Natlanese people go there when they die and slowly lose themselves into a sea of souls. Living warriors can draw on those Nightsouls to enhance their abilities, which is Nightsoul's Blessing.

The Night Kingdom effectively works as Natlan's Ley Lines. Natlan lacks stable, deep Ley Lines, and the original ones were badly damaged in the War of Funerary Flame. The Lord of the Night, guided by Ronova, rebuilt a similar network from the fragments; the first Pyro Archon, Xbalanque, strengthened it later. Memories gained in Natlan are recorded there. Experiences outside Natlan are not, which is why Xilonen needed the Lord of the Night's help to forge an Ancient Name for the Traveler.

Wayob and night kingdom: The Wayob are described by the Dreamseeker Priest as non-corporeal "will without form or thought." They live in the Night Kingdom and can see the past and future. Each tribe has its own Wayob, and the Wayob choose who receives an Ancient Name. They are not physically in Natlan, but they can appear through obsidian totems and Nightsouls as Wayob Manifestations. Natlan's people do not know why these appear; the common belief is that they are sent to solve some problem.

Ancient names and death: Ancient Names are obsidian-stone titles carried by chosen members of the tribes. Their deeds become part of the Name's legacy. Each is granted by a tribe's Wayob to someone who has lived out its spirit, or is forged on commission of the Pyro Archon by a Name Engraver at a cost to the smith's lifespan. A bearer who fell in the Night Warden Wars can be returned by the Ode of Resurrection if their group won against the Abyss. If no one returned victorious, the Name is lost for good. A bearer who dies in some other way is reborn in Natlan eventually, in another form.

Known uses: Entering the state boosts mobility and fighting power; characters often move in ways ordinary people cannot. Kachina, for instance, rides Turbo Twirly while she has points left, and the state ends when they run out.

Nightsoul Transmission lets a Natlan character swiftly run, climb, swim or jump after a swap. Nightsoul Burst is a periodic surge triggered by elemental damage when a Natlanese character is in the party. Nightsoul points are gained or spent by each character in their own way; when they run out or when certain abilities are used, Phlogiston is drawn instead.

Limits: It is a Natlan power: it works best in Natlan and relies on the Night Kingdom's support.

The state ends when a character's Nightsoul points are exhausted. The Night Kingdom has no record of deeds outside Natlan, and in canon the Wayob protect their people poorly abroad.

Interactions: Phlogiston: Natlan's primordial energy, a form of Pyro, powers many Natlan devices and Saurian abilities, and is drawn on when Nightsoul points are gone.

Visions and the Elements: Nightsoul's Blessing is not an element, so it rides on whatever element a character wields. Burning is a fast way to wear down a Void Ward without the state.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): the state is entered mainly through Elemental Skills, enhances movement and combat, and is boosted in Natlan. Nightsoul Burst triggers on elemental damage with an interval of 18 seconds for one Natlanese character in the party, 12 for two and 9 for three or more, marked by a white screen outline. The mechanics arrived with Natlan in Version 5.0.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show it as quiet weight: ember-lit patterns of soul-light, a sense of ancestors close by, a body suddenly lighter. Natlanese characters treat it as ordinary inheritance and take it with humour or pride. Keep respect for the dead.

161.content: The Night Kingdom is the realm of the Wayob and the souls of Natlan's dead, made by Yohualtecuhtin, the Lord of the Night, from fragments of the old Ley Lines, and it serves as Natlan's Ley Lines. Natlanese souls lose themselves there into a sea of souls. Souls of warriors who die in Natlan's ritual wars can be recalled by the Ode of Resurrection if their group wins.

162.content: The Wayob are the spirits of the six tribes, believed to embody the will of tribal ancestors. They guard their people and choose who bears an Ancient Name. They can appear in Natlan as obsidian-tied Wayob Manifestations, which are also elite enemies in play.

163.content: An Ancient Name is a title and a stone representing the deeds of all its past bearers, chosen by a Wayob or forged on the Pyro Archon's commission. If a bearer dies in the Night Warden Wars and nobody in the group returns victorious, the Name is lost.

164.content: A periodic surge that triggers when a party containing a Natlanese character deals elemental damage. On its own it does nothing; some talents and artifacts add effects.

165.content:
Overloaded (also: Overloaded reaction, Overloaded DMG, Pyro-Electro reaction): Overloaded is the elemental reaction between Pyro and Electro, in either order. It causes an explosion that deals area Pyro damage and throws nearby targets back. It is a combat rule, so treat it as a gameplay abstraction that a scene may borrow from, not a named law of the world.

Overloaded has existed since Version 1.0. It is a transformative reaction, meaning it deals its own damage separate from the attack that triggered it. The in-game tutorial calls it a powerful explosion and tells players to alternate Pyro and Electro attacks to trigger it.

In universe: Canon gives no story explanation for Overloaded. The in-game tutorial only says that when Pyro meets Electro, or Electro meets Pyro, Overloaded occurs, causing powerful explosions that deal area Pyro damage.

Nothing read ties the reaction to a character, god or event. Do not invent an origin. Fire and lightning causing a blast is a natural image for a scene, but treat it as flavour.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Overloaded happens when Electro hits a target carrying Pyro, or Pyro hits a target carrying Electro. The explosion deals area Pyro damage in a roughly 5 metre radius and causes strong knockback.

- It does not apply Pyro to the targets it hits, so it cannot set off further reactions by itself.
- Overloaded damage counts as a blunt attack, so it can trigger Shatter on Frozen targets and is more effective against certain enemy shields.
- Like other transformative reactions, its damage depends on the level of the character who triggers it and is raised by that character's Elemental Mastery. It cannot CRIT.

Limits: Overloaded needs both elements on the same target and does nothing to a target with only one. The knockback can scatter enemies instead of keeping them together.

The explosion is fixed-size and tied to the triggering character's level, so a weak character does not produce a huge blast. Pyro-immune enemies reduce its damage.

Examples: Gameplay example from the in-game tutorial: switch characters in battle and use Pyro and Electro attacks in turn to trigger Overloaded and defeat opponents quickly. The wiki's preview shows an Overloaded blast on an enemy and one used to break open ore.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show Overloaded as a sharp bang of purple lightning and orange flame, with a shockwave that shoves people and loose objects back. Keep it a single blast, loud and brief, not a lasting fire.

166.content:
Party (also: Party Setup, party system, character switching, team composition): A party is a team of up to four playable characters. The player controls one at a time and can swap to another with a short delay. Team bonuses such as Elemental Resonance apply to the party as a whole.

The ability to set up parties unlocks after the quest "Unexpected Power".

In universe: Gameplay abstraction: in the story the Traveler travels with a handful of friends, but canon never states a four-person limit or an instant swap between them. Treat party swapping as the game's way of presenting who is fighting rather than a rule of the world.

Gameplay: Gameplay: switching characters has a 1-second cooldown. Up to four characters are deployed, added left to right, and a team with none cannot be deployed. Trial-character stages can add a fifth, the trial character, to a full party of four.

Party Setup is opened from the Paimon Menu or with L on PC. There are four default teams ("Party 1" to "Party 4"), which can be renamed but not disbanded, and a maximum of 15 teams. The deployed team cannot be disbanded. Characters can be reordered by dragging, and the Configure Team and Quick Setup menus help manage them. The Party Setup background can change by region, with variants for Nod-Krai (also depending on Moonsign characters) and Snezhnaya (depending on Stellar Linchpin characters), if the player enables that setting.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay (this project's interpretation, not canon): in fiction, the Traveler's friends take turns in a fight and cover for each other. Avoid telling characters they have been "swapped out"; treat it as people stepping in and out of a battle.

Limits: The four-character limit, cooldown and menu are mechanics. Canon does not limit how many friends the Traveler may have around them.

167.content:
Phlogiston (also: primal flame, Natlan Phlogiston, Liquid Phlogiston, Solid Phlogiston, Gaseous Phlogiston): Phlogiston is the primal energy of Natlan. People there can sense and use it: it powers machines, written signs and the Nightsoul's Blessing state of Natlan's warriors. It exists as liquid, solid and gaseous forms and flows along Spiritways. Canon calls it Teyvat's primordial energy and a form of "computronium", programmable matter that stores information. The dragon Kukulkan stole it and taught humans to use it.

The Heavenly Principles later reworked elemental energy using phlogiston as a base, so elemental energy is described as phlogiston's modern counterpart. Natlanese treat phlogiston as a symbol of an indomitable spirit.

In universe: In the world: Natlan's people use phlogiston for devices, signs, paints and warrior abilities. It carries heat and is dangerous to those who cannot handle it, but the Natlanese, nearly all of whom can use it, read it and work with it directly.

Phlogiston can appear as a gas that leaks from the ground and flows in currents, as a flowing liquid, and as solid crystals or blocks. Natlanese craft solid phlogiston into barrels, targets and nails. Item text describes it as a high-temperature thermal energy found throughout Natlan "in all shapes and sizes", and warriors switch to drawing on it to keep their Nightsoul's Blessing going once their Nightsoul runs out.

Origins: Phlogiston is one of Teyvat's ancient forms of energy. In the Archon Quest "Beneath the Secret Source" (5.1), the Lord of the Night explains that phlogiston is Teyvat's primordial energy, that it belongs to the Light Realm, and that elemental energy is built on it: as he puts it, light splits into seven colours like a rainbow, and elemental energy is a similar idea, the modern counterpart of phlogiston. The Heavenly Principles developed it to counter the Abyss better.

Dragons and computronium: In the world quest "An Omen of Annihilation and the Final Entreaty" (5.5), Kukulkan tells the Traveler that phlogiston is an atom on which information can be written, a form of "computronium" that can imitate the essence of anything through the weaving of language, which is why it takes on different forms. The ancient dragons used it this way. Their golden script, Iridescent Inscriptions, works as a programming language for phlogiston: it records information, controls Secret Source mechanisms, converts phlogiston between forms, creates Spiritways and lets dragons reshape their own appearance.

Kukulkan and humans: The dragon Kukulkan, called the Sage of the Stolen Flame, took phlogiston from his kin and taught humans in Natlan to use it. Natlanese tradition names him the origin of their ability to use it.

Forms: Gaseous, liquid and solid phlogiston, and Spiritways.

- Gaseous: free-flowing heat, leaking from the ground or forming currents and wind tunnels. It burns those who cannot handle it.
- Liquid: a molten flow that ignites those who touch it, but is safe for Saurians of certain kinds and certain characters.
- Solid: orange crystals or blocks used for tools and barriers.
- Spiritway: a flowing channel carrying travellers in the Nightsoul's Blessing state.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Phlogiston is a shared party meter in Natlan, capped at 100. It is consumed once Nightsoul points run out and by Saurian Indwelling abilities, and it is refilled by collecting items, breaking objects and standing near certain features. It is not available in domains.

Fatui extraction: The Fatui run a secret underground base in Natlan's Coatepec Mountain, the Phlogiston Extraction Research Center, where they extract phlogiston from captured Saurians. Fontaine Research Institute equipment is used there, though it is unclear how much the Institute knows about what it is used for. A soldier's diary in the base says the soldiers do not know the purpose of the research.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1, phlogiston remains Natlan's central energy resource and symbol. No later canon found in the Nod-Krai or Snezhnaya chapters changes what is said above. Huitzilopochtli is covered in its own entry.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): treat phlogiston as the everyday lifeblood of Natlan: warm, flowing, taken for granted by locals and alarming to outsiders who step into it. Natlanese characters sense it the way others sense a smell, so they notice engravings, leaks and Saurians' condition without tools. Outsiders from other nations should treat liquid or gaseous phlogiston as dangerous.

168.content: Iridescent Inscriptions are the golden script the ancient dragons of Natlan used to wield phlogiston, essentially a programming language for matter. Humans imitated it as Phlogiston Engravings, which can store text, build Spiritdoors and Phlogiston Chiseliths, and underlie Ancient Name carving and Nightspirit graffiti.

169.content: A secret Fatui base under Coatepec Mountain where phlogiston is extracted from captured Saurians. It uses Fontaine Research Institute equipment. Staff there write that the purpose of the research was never explained to them.

170.comment: Phlogiston: Liquid and gaseous Phlogiston hazards
170.content: Liquid phlogiston burns those who enter it, gaseous phlogiston burns those who stand in its currents, and solid phlogiston forms crystals and blocks used for devices. Qucusaurs and some Flower-Feather Clan members have mastered gaseous phlogiston without being burned, and Koholasaurs and certain characters move through liquid phlogiston safely.

171.content:
Physical (also: Physical damage, Physical DMG, non-elemental damage): Physical is the eighth damage type in Genshin Impact: ordinary force with no element in it, such as a sword cut, a hammer blow or a crushing impact. The other seven damage types are the elements. Physical has no Archon, nation or Vision. It is a game category rather than a power the story names.

Elemental reactions are built from the seven elements, so Physical normally sits outside them. The main exception is Shatter, which deals Physical damage.

In universe: Canon never presents Physical as a force or Authority. In the story, a strike without elemental energy is just a strike: steel, muscle, teeth, claws or falling stone.

This is the main difference from the elements. The elements are tied to Visions, Gnoses, Archons and the Dragon Sovereigns, while Physical has nothing comparable. In narration, treat "Physical" as the absence of elemental energy, not as an eighth element.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Sword, Claymore and Polearm attacks deal Physical DMG by default. So do Bow Normal Attacks and Aimed Shots that are not fully charged. Catalyst attacks are inherently elemental, so Catalyst users deal Physical DMG only through extra effects.

Some Elemental Skills and Bursts also deal Physical DMG. The wiki's examples are Eula's Glacial Illumination, Xinyan's Riff Revolution and Freminet's Pressurized Floe. Physical DMG Bonus is a stat, found as a character ascension stat, a weapon substat or an artifact bonus (for instance the 2-piece bonus of Bloodstained Chivalry or Pale Flame, +25%). Physical RES is the matching defence. Enemies can deal Physical damage too; the Stonehide Lawachurl's punches, charge and slam are examples.

Limits: Physical does not react with any element and applies no aura.

No Vision or Gnosis grants Physical power. A character cannot "have a Physical element".

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show Physical as weight, edge and momentum: a clean cut, a heavy blow, ground shaking from a slam. It has no signature colour or glow, and nothing about it needs special explanation.

172.content: Shatter is the reaction in which a blunt hit (a Claymore attack, for example) or a Geo attack lands on a target frozen by the Frozen reaction. The ice breaks and the hit deals Physical damage. See the Shattered entry for the full reaction.

173.content: Physical RES reduces incoming Physical damage. Protective Canopy resonance, certain talents, constellations, artifacts and dishes can raise it. Superconduct lowers an enemy's Physical RES by 40% for 12 seconds, and some talents, constellations and artifacts can lower it too.

174.content:
Prime Ice (also: Prime Ice Construct, Prime Ice Constructs, Prime Ice Resource, Fab-Vision): Prime Ice is a pale ice found across Snezhnaya that does not melt like ordinary frost. The Traveler can harvest it with the Fab-Vision function of the Eye of Graeae to gain Prime Ice Resource, then spend that resource, plus Kresnik Energy, to build Prime Ice Constructs: heat sources, grappling hooks, launch pads and more. Constructs can be taken down again for a refund of the ice.

It is introduced in the Archon Quest "Into the Wind, Into the Frigid North" (7.0), where the Eye of Graeae teaches the Traveler to clear blocking ice and prop up a door with a cube. It is an exploration tool, not a combat element.

In universe: In-world, Prime Ice is a durable ice native to Snezhnaya. The townsfolk of Svetloledovka make a living by harvesting it. Ordinary humans cannot shape it, but Snowland Fae can manipulate it naturally.

The Eye of Graeae, a device-bound entity, is the Traveler's way of working it. It tells the Traveler that constructs last only briefly and cannot be stabilised during the development period, so it was allowed to use Kresnik Kristall as a heat source. The Eye also says it has forgotten what warmth feels like. Item text describes the glaciafruit, a star-shaped fruit, as born from Prime Ice after a peculiar change in the permafrost, "for reasons unknown".

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Fab-Vision is a mode of the Eye of Graeae gadget, usable in Snezhnaya while running, falling or fighting but not while gliding or swimming. Harvesting a deposit gives Prime Ice Resource (most deposits roughly 15 to 70 units; the largest are rare, often do not respawn and fill the 400-unit storage). Building spends resource and a percentage of Kresnik Energy; removing a construct refunds the resource.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): treat the Eye of Graeae's tools as a craft, not magic anyone can learn. The Traveler can spend the Eye's stored resource to raise a wall, a stair or a warm brazier, and gives the material back by taking the thing down. Describe pale, hard ice that shapes quickly under Fab-Vision and stays cold to the touch. Keep scale small: bridges, hooks and braziers, not fortresses.

Limits: Prime Ice constructs can only be built in Snezhnaya using the Eye of Graeae. Each type has a limit per area, and the Traveler can only carry 400 units of resource.

Fab-Vision cannot be used while gliding or swimming. Kresnik Energy is needed to build, and is used up faster in colder zones. Constructs cannot be stacked or placed where the player is standing.

175.content: A Prime Ice Construct is any object the Traveler builds from Prime Ice Resource with the Eye of Graeae, unlocked by blueprints. They are short-lived by design, can be removed for a refund, and many gain extra effects inside a Polestar Field. The first constructs the Traveler learns are the Cube and the Basic Heat Source.

176.content: Prime Ice Resource is the material stored in the Eye of Graeae's internal reservoir. Item text says it can be used to build the mechanisms and constructs in the blueprints. It is gained by harvesting Prime Ice or deconstructing constructs, and the gadget holds at most 400 units.

177.content: Glaciafruit is a star-shaped fruit that grows from a Prime Ice branch on the Snezhnayan tundra. Taking the branch away with the Eye of Graeae drops the fruit into the snow and returns a little Prime Ice Resource. Item text says it forms from Prime Ice for reasons unknown; it is edible and used in cooking.

178.content:
Pyro (also: Pyro element, element of fire, Pyro Archon's element): Pyro is the element of fire, one of Teyvat's seven elements. Its Archon is the God of War and bears the divine name Haborym; the current Pyro Archon is Mavuika, who rules Natlan, the land of Pyro. Unlike other Archons, Pyro Archons are mortals who win the throne in battle. People with Pyro Visions ignite, burn and explode things. The Pyro Gnosis never reached the Fatui; as of 7.1 it has vanished.

Pyro ascension gems are Agnidus Agates. Natlan's Statues of The Seven take Pyroculi. The Pyro Archon looks after the Sacred Flame, the fire that protects Natlan and its warriors.

In universe: Most people use Pyro through a Vision. A Pyro Archon draws on the Sacred Flame and the Pyro Archon's divine throne instead. In Natlan the element is bound up with war, oaths and the idea that humans can become gods.

Natlan's culture treats fire as something earned in contest. Contending Fire, the energy produced when Natlanese warriors fight each other, fuels the Sacred Flame, especially through the Pilgrimage of the Return of the Sacred Flame. Objects carried in battle can also become soaked with Contending Fire and be burned to feed it. Elsewhere in Teyvat, Pyro is the ordinary element of campfires, forges, kitchens and fireworks.

Archon and nation: Archon: the Pyro Archon, God of War among The Seven, divine name Haborym. Current holder: Mavuika. Nation: Natlan.

Every Pyro Archon begins as a human and wins the position through battle. They stay mortal: they age and die, so Natlan has had many Pyro Archons. When a new one takes the divine throne, an inner flame awakens and the Sacred Flame hands them deep knowledge and memory of the land. They are also charged with protecting and fuelling the Sacred Flame.

Gnosis and authority: A Gnosis is a device that resonates directly with Celestia and is more advanced than a Vision. Seven were made, one per element. The Pyro Gnosis was the one Capitano of the Fatui first pursued, but his duel with Mavuika ended inconclusively and he changed course, so the Fatui never retrieved it. Mavuika had long refused to use it, because rewriting the ley lines with it would erase Natlan's history.

Elemental beings: Xiuhcoatl, the Pyro Dragon Sovereign, and Pyro lifeforms such as Pyro slimes, specters, Abyss Mages, the Pyro Hypostasis and the Pyro Regisvine.

Pyro Slimes are described as small monsters formed by Pyro settling throughout nature. Pyro Specters are born from highly concentrated Pyro and float in the air; an Akademiya student reportedly argued they were a kind of Crystalfly, and has not graduated. Pyro Abyss Mages command Pyro and can communicate with hilichurls, so they manipulate them easily.

Known uses: Igniting and burning things, explosions, heating, cooking and forging, and fire-based attacks. Pyro also melts ice and boils water in many fights.

In Natlan, Pyro is also a way to carry names and promises: objects carried in battle become imbued with Contending Fire and can be burned as fuel, as Mavuika does with her keepsakes, and Pyro Archons move the dead through the Sacred Flame during the Ode of Resurrection, stepping into the flame and returning with the fallen warrior.

Limits: Pyro does not react with Pyro. It does little on its own against water or ice.

Pyro needs a Vision or an Archon's authority; ordinary fire is just fire. Keep scale proportionate to the source.

Interactions: Vaporize with Hydro, Melt with Cryo, Overloaded with Electro, Burning with Dendro, Swirl with Anemo and Crystallize with Geo.

Vaporize amplifies damage when Pyro or Hydro triggers it; Melt does so with Cryo. Overloaded is an explosion with strong knockback. Burning keeps Pyro damage ticking in a small area around a target while a Dendro aura exists. Swirl spreads Pyro to nearby enemies. Crystallize makes a Pyro shard that grants a Pyro shield. Burgeon is Pyro detonating a Dendro Core created by Bloom.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Pyro is a damage type and the element of Pyro Vision holders. The Elemental Resonance Fervent Flames (two or more Pyro characters in a party) shortens Cryo's effect by 40% and raises ATK by 25%.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show Pyro as heat, light and sound: air shimmering, embers drifting, sudden warmth, crackle. Warm orange and red are safe visual cues. In Natlan, fire reads as honour, contest and shared meals rather than just destruction.

179.content: The Pyro Archon is the God of War among The Seven and the ruler of Natlan. The divine name Haborym is linked to the position. Every Pyro Archon starts as a human who wins the position by battle and remains mortal. Mavuika, who is both the current Pyro Archon and the one who held the throne at the Cataclysm, is covered by her own entry.

180.content: The Pyro Gnosis was never collected by the Fatui. Mavuika, who had always refused to use it, passed it through the Traveler so Nahida could burn the corrupted Irminsul in 6.6. It then disappeared. Mavuika sensed it go; its exact fate is not stated.

181.content: The Sacred Flame is a fire that burns continually in the Stadium of the Sacred Flame. It is a conduit to the Night Kingdom and the Wayob, and a base of Natlan's resistance to the Abyss. It is fuelled by Contending Fire from combat between Natlanese warriors. Smaller flames split from it are used in rituals such as the Scions of the Canopy's Turnfire Night.

182.content:
Quicken (also: Quicken reaction, Quickened, Quicken Aura, Catalyze, Catalyze reactions, Dendro-Electro reaction): Quicken is the elemental reaction between Dendro and Electro, in either order. It deals no damage itself. It leaves the target Quickened, with a Quicken Aura that decays over time. While the aura lasts, further Dendro or Electro hits on the target trigger the Spread or Aggravate reactions, which add bonus damage to those hits. It is a combat rule, so treat it as a gameplay abstraction, not a named law of the world.

Quicken appeared with Version 3.0 and the Dendro element, along with Sumeru. The wiki treats Quicken, Aggravate and Spread as one group called Catalyze. Spread and Aggravate have their own entries (system.spread, system.aggravate).

In universe: Canon gives no story explanation for Quicken. The in-game tutorial only says that when creatures are affected by Electro and Dendro, Quicken occurs and renders them Quickened, and that Quickened creatures hit by Electro or Dendro suffer additional damage through Aggravate or Spread.

Nothing read ties the reaction to a character, god or event. Do not invent an origin or a mechanism.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Quicken happens when Dendro hits a target carrying Electro, or Electro hits a target carrying Dendro. It applies a Quicken Aura to the target, and the reaction itself deals no damage.

- A target with a Quicken Aura that is hit by Dendro triggers Spread, and by Electro triggers Aggravate. Each gives the hit a flat damage bonus added to its base damage. Spread's bonus is slightly larger than Aggravate's.
- Spread and Aggravate do not consume the Quicken Aura, so a team can keep triggering them while it lasts.
- Pyro or Hydro applied to a Quicken Aura consumes it, triggering Burning or Bloom respectively.
- Quicken Aura can coexist with Electro and Dendro auras on the same target.

Limits: Quicken deals nothing by itself and needs both Dendro and Electro to be applied. It does not apply to plants that are not Dendro; "Wood" objects such as vines cannot trigger it.

Quicken only helps Dendro and Electro attacks. Pyro or Hydro attacks on the aura end it. Because attacks have an internal cooldown on applying their element, a source cannot apply Dendro or Electro on every hit.

Examples: Gameplay example: an Electro attack lands on a target already covered in Dendro, and the target is Quickened. A Dendro character then strikes it for Spread, and an Electro character for Aggravate, both for extra damage.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show Quicken as purple and green energy crawling over the target, like vines humming with charge, which makes later strikes bite harder. It reads as a setup: an unresolved charge waiting for another strike.

183.content: Catalyze is the wiki's name for the Dendro-Electro group of reactions: Quicken, which applies the aura, and Spread and Aggravate, which are the bonus-damage reactions triggered by hits on a Quickened target. The tutorial in the game is titled Elemental Reaction: Catalyze. Its English wiki page covers all three.

184.content: Spread is triggered by a Dendro hit on a Quickened target, and Aggravate by an Electro hit. Both add a flat bonus to the triggering hit's base damage and do not consume the Quicken Aura. Spread's bonus is slightly higher. Each has its own entry (system.spread, system.aggravate).

185.content:
Physical laws and roleplay physics (also: roleplay physics, Teyvat physics, physical laws of Teyvat): This entry tells a narrator how physical reality works in Teyvat roleplay. The default is ordinary human biology and consequences: people eat, sleep, tire, are hurt and recover slowly, and death is permanent unless a specific canon mechanism applies. Visions, Archons, adepti and ancient powers are exceptions with limits. Game mechanics (health bars, respawning at a Statue of The Seven, instant fast travel) are abstractions, not literal in-world rules. Each section below separates what canon shows from this project's recommended reading.

Rule of thumb: when canon shows a rule, follow it; when canon is silent, assume the real-world answer for a pre-industrial setting with magic added only where a source supports it; never let a character do something because "it is a game".

Ordinary biology: Canon: ordinary people in Teyvat are shown living as humans do: they work, eat, rest and fall ill. Recommended: treat ordinary NPCs and Vision holders alike as physically human, with normal needs for food, water, sleep and shelter. A Vision grants control over one element, not toughness, immunity or freedom from need.

Canon shows food and drink at the centre of daily life across the nations, and food is used to restore strength in the game. Recommended: hunger, thirst, fatigue and cold should matter on long journeys, and the narrator should avoid hand-waving them unless the scene is brief. Do not add specifics (calorie needs, sleep hours) as canon.

Ageing and lifespans: Canon: no source gives a human lifespan. Ordinary people age. Long-lived beings exist but are not ordinary: the adepti are extremely long-lived or immortal by enlightenment; pure-blooded Khaenri'ahns were cursed with immortality; Pyro Archons, unlike other Archons, are mortals who age and die like humans.

Medicine and healing: Canon: medicine in Teyvat mixes herbal remedies with more advanced care, including surgery, bandages, setting dislocations, injected medicines and some recognition of mental illness and therapy. Elemental power can heal: Barbara is a known Hydro healer and Jean has healed with Anemo. Manipulating the elemental energy in a body has been used experimentally to control Eleazar's symptoms and is not widespread.

Injury and recovery: Canon shows wounds, scars, poisoning and illness, and that recovery takes time. Recommended: injuries stay with a character until they plausibly heal; an injured character fights worse, moves slower or rests; a serious wound is not erased between scenes.

Death: Canon: death is real and usually permanent. Gods and Archons can die: Decarabian fell, Rukkhadevata and the Belyi Tsar died in past struggles against the Abyss, and Ronova died during the story. Recommended: a character who dies in a roleplay stays dead unless a canon mechanism below applies and the story earns it.

Gameplay (not literal lore): a "fallen" character is revived at a Statue of The Seven, by a dish or by a constellation; if the whole party falls, it is restored at the nearest waypoint at low health. This is a rule of the game, not of the world. Recommended: do not treat death as a setback that resets; the narrator may fade to a rescue or a near-death, but should say so.

Resurrection: Canon shows only a few bounded forms: the Natlan Ode of Resurrection, adepti raising Qiqi as a zombie, and the cursed immortality of the Khaenri'ahns. None is a general fix for death.

Qiqi was mortally wounded, then resurrected by the adepti as a zombie, which required sealing her in amber because the adeptal energy overwhelmed her. She has trouble keeping memories, has no sense of smell and no strong emotions, prefers cold, and her flesh decays in heat. Recommended: resurrection costs something lasting.

Water and pressure: Canon: in Fontaine, the power of the Transoceanic Sourcewater lets Vision holders (and others such as the Traveler and Paimon) breathe and speak underwater. People without Visions rely on diving gear and specialised training. Archenoul says adapting to water pressure is a concern for non-Vision holders, which implies it is not for Vision holders. Outside that context there is no breathing-underwater rule.

Limits: This entry does not give a statistical system and does not replace character or location entries. Where an individual entry states a power, a condition or a lifespan, that entry takes priority over the general guidance here.

186.comment: Physical laws and roleplay physics: Ode of Resurrection
186.content: The Ode of Resurrection is a Natlan ceremony at the Stadium of the Sacred Flame that raises Ancient Name bearers who died fighting the Abyss in the Night Warden Wars, provided their group achieved victory. It heals only fatal injuries. The Pyro Archon enters the Sacred Flame to seek the deceased and their Ancient Name in the Night Kingdom. It failed for Kachina; later Mavuika extended it to all of Natlan's warriors with the Lord of the Night's power, and it ended after the Night Wars.

187.comment: Physical laws and roleplay physics: Dragonspine cold
187.content: Dragonspine, formerly Vindagnyr, has an extreme cold climate that built up after the Skyfrost Nail destroyed the ley line tree on the mountain. Grass does not burn there, and the cold weakens travellers over time unless they keep warm. Snezhnaya has comparable cold zones. Recommended: describe it as dangerous exposure requiring shelter, fire and food.

188.comment: Physical laws and roleplay physics: Transoceanic Sourcewater
188.content: In Fontaine, the Transoceanic Sourcewater lets Vision holders, the Traveler and Paimon breathe and speak underwater. People without Visions use diving gear and specialised training, and water pressure is a concern for them. Do not carry this over to other nations.

189.comment: Physical laws and roleplay physics: Curse of immortality
189.content: During the Cataclysm, Ronova placed a curse of immortality on pure-blooded Khaenri'ahns, which the wiki describes as a punishment. Dainsleif is also immortal; his brother Vedrfolnir gave him a ring that continuously resets his body's condition, but his mind is still affected by erosion. Immortality in canon is a burden, not a reward.

190.comment: Physical laws and roleplay physics: Teleportation limits
190.content: Canon is unclear about how Teleport Waypoints work. Leifhelm says his Grand Master crossed from Nod-Krai to Mondstadt along the Ley Lines quickly, and the Fatui and Mona use teleportation in quests. Recommended: treat teleportation as rare and tied to a device or power.

191.comment: Physical laws and roleplay physics: Zombie condition
191.content: Qiqi was resurrected as a zombie by the adepti after being mortally wounded, and sealed in amber because the energy was too much for her. She has trouble retaining memories, lacks a sense of smell, shows little emotion, prefers cold and decays in heat. Use this as the template for how canon treats the cost of resurrection.

192.content:
Saurian Indwelling (also: indwelling a Saurian, indwelt Saurian, Spiritsconce, Spiritsconces): Saurian Indwelling is an ability of the Traveler in Natlan: their spirit slips into a Saurian (one of Natlan's dragon-kin) and acts through its body, so they can run, climb, glide or swim as that creature does. The in-game tutorial credits "a mysterious power" with the gift. It is not presented as a Vision or an Archon's power, and almost nobody else in Natlan seems to know it exists.

It works on Saurians of the six tribal species and on small totem-like markers called Spiritsconces, and it ends when the Traveler chooses to leave or the body is lost. Each species brings its own movement and elemental strike, so indwelling is how the Traveler crosses ground that a human on foot could not.

In universe: Natlan's Saurians are descendants of Pyro vishaps that lost their ancient intelligence; they follow emotion and trust their human companions. Tribe members learn to read a Saurian's moods through long companionship. Indwelling is different: the Traveler's spirit enters the animal, and while inside, the speech of Saurians becomes understandable to them. Nobody is shown teaching the Traveler this; it simply works.

The Traveler first indwells a Saurian in the World Quest "Lost in the Woods" (5.0). Brought into a strange golden space on arrival in Natlan, they and Paimon find a weakened adult Tepetlisaurus and a whelp, later named Little One, caught in trouble. The Traveler's body vanishes and the adult rises with new energy; Paimon realises the Traveler is "inside" it. The Traveler uses it to free the whelp. Later, people who notice the effect do not understand it: Chasca sensed that an indwelt Qucusaur had the Traveler's demeanour but chose not to ask, and Coyllur found the Traveler oddly familiar after first meeting them as a Qucusaur.

Spiritsconces: Spiritsconces are small, colourful totems found across Natlan. Saurians are described as able to enter a "Spiritsconce" state under particular circumstances; indwelling one lets the Traveler take on the Saurian's original form. When the Traveler leaves a Saurian without killing it, a Spiritsconce is left where they stood, and defeated adult Saurians leave one too.

Species and abilities: Each tribe's Saurian offers its own way of moving, tied to an element and to its tribe's land.
- Tepetlisaurus (Geo): burrows and climbs rock at speed; home of the Children of Echoes.
- Yumkasaurus (Dendro): grapples and glides, grabs and spits out objects; Scions of the Canopy.
- Koholasaurus (Hydro): swims and dashes through water and Liquid Phlogiston; People of the Springs.
- Qucusaurus (Pyro): flies and dives; Flower-Feather Clan.
- Iktomisaurus (Cryo): glides, high jumps, and can scan and place Nightspirit Graffiti objects; Masters of the Night-Wind.
- Tatankasaurus (Electro): charges, smashes Pulverite and pushes heavy objects; Collective of Plenty.

Limits: Some creatures refuse. A few quest-linked Saurians, such as "Half-Baked" in "Special Friends", reject the attempt with a message that a strong will refuses the indwelling. Indwelt Saurians are poor fighters and cannot dash to dodge attacks.

A Saurian is forced out if it tries to enter the main settlement of a tribe that is not its own: the screen warns that outside Saurians may not enter, and the Traveler is ejected. Only the matching species is allowed in each tribe's home (Tepetlisaurus for the Children of Echoes, and so on, as listed above). Per the wiki, runes bar outsiders, and who made them is unexplained. Leaving Natlan's boundaries, teleporting or entering instance rooms also ends the indwelling. While indwelling, the Traveler cannot cook, use a Statue of The Seven, or use a Tablet of Tona.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): indwelling is an exploration mechanic introduced with Natlan in 5.0. An indwelt Saurian uses its own Phlogiston meter before the player's. Phlogiston is refilled near Everflame Seeds, Teleport Waypoints and Statues of The Seven, by touching Flaming Seeds of Phlogiston, and by collecting or smashing certain items. All indwelt Saurians share the same stats. While indwelling, NPCs other than Saurians usually say only "..." except for quest-specific dialogue. Indwelling counts as leaving combat only if the indwelt enemy was the sole aggravated one.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): treat indwelling as a quiet, uncanny act. The Traveler's body goes still or seems to vanish and the Saurian moves with unusual purpose and awareness. Natlanese who see it should be puzzled rather than certain; they might sense something familiar about the animal without naming it.

193.content: A Spiritsconce is a small, colourful totem-like marker left behind in Natlan. Saurians can enter a "Spiritsconce" state in particular circumstances, and the Traveler can indwell one to take on the Saurian's original form. Leaving a Saurian alive, or defeating an adult one, leaves a Spiritsconce behind.

194.content: Each Saurian group has its own main territory, which neighbouring Saurians respect; entry is by a local Saurian's invitation and escort. The same borders broadly mark the lands of the Natlanese tribes. In play, an indwelt Saurian tries to enter a rival tribe's village and the Traveler is ejected; the wiki says canon explains this with runes whose origin is unknown. Little One, the Tepetlisaurus whelp, alone slips through those of the Collective of Plenty, perhaps because of the volcano's instability or the Flamelord's Blessing (unconfirmed).

195.content:
Shattered (also: Shatter, Shattered reaction, Shatter reaction): Shatter, listed in the wiki's reaction list as Shattered, is the follow-up to Frozen. When a frozen target is hit by a blunt attack or a Geo attack, the ice breaks apart, the Freeze Aura is removed, and the target takes Physical damage.

It has been part of the game since 1.0 along with Frozen, which has to happen first. Hydro and Cryo together make a target Frozen; a heavy or Geo strike then shatters it.

In universe: Canon gives no in-world explanation for Shatter. The pages read treat it as a combat rule, so it is best understood as the ordinary physical fact that frozen things break when hit hard.

Gameplay: Gameplay: a Frozen target hit by a blunt attack (a claymore swing, a heavy hammer strike) or by Geo takes Shatter damage, and the Freeze Aura ends.

- Shatter deals Physical damage and is a transformative reaction: it has its own base damage set by the reaction type and the level of the character who triggers it, and that damage is raised by Elemental Mastery. It cannot critically strike, is not based on ATK, and is reduced by the target's resistance.
- Shatter happens before any elemental damage in the same hit, which can prevent some other reactions.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show a crack running through a coating of ice, a sharp snap, and a spray of fragments flying outwards. A Geo strike should feel like a stone slamming into the ice; a claymore should feel like a heavy hammer blow.

Limits: Shatter needs a Frozen target and a blunt or Geo hit. Weak physical strikes may not be enough.

It removes the Freeze Aura, so it ends the Frozen state. Pyro, Electro or Anemo on a Freeze Aura trigger Melt, Superconduct or Swirl instead.

Examples: Gameplay example, from the in-game tutorial: soak an opponent with Hydro, switch to a Cryo character to freeze them, then strike with a Geo or blunt attack to Shatter.

196.content: Frozen is the Hydro-Cryo reaction that immobilises a target with a Freeze Aura. Shatter is the follow-up that breaks that aura with a blunt or Geo hit. See system.frozen for the full rule set, resistance and immunity.

197.content:
Shield (also: Shields, character shield, Crystallize shield): A shield is a barrier that takes damage in place of a character's HP. Characters gain them by collecting Crystallize shards or through certain talents, Constellations and weapons. Most are elemental and resist their own element especially well. Enemies have separate shields called wards.

Shield Strength is the stat that makes a character's shields hold up better.

In universe: In the world, shields appear as protective barriers: a wall of crystal or stone, a sheath of an element, or a bubble of energy. Characters do not speak of Shield Strength or absorption bonuses.

Crystallize shards come from a Crystallize reaction, and the Geovishap Hatchling is a creature whose Geo shards give a Geo shield on contact.

Gameplay: Gameplay: damage hits the shield's health first, and only the excess reaches the character. A shield that times out is destroyed, which can trigger effects such as Kachina's Constellation. If a character has several shields, one hit affects all of them at once.

Elemental shields absorb their own element at 250 percent, so they take only 40 percent as much damage from it. Geo shields absorb every damage type at 150 percent. Crystallize shields get health from the level and Elemental Mastery of whoever caused the reaction. Talent and Constellation shields usually scale with DEF, ATK, Max HP or Elemental Mastery, and some add further absorption that multiplies with the base bonus.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay (this project's interpretation, not canon): describe a shield as a visible barrier of crystal, stone or elemental energy that breaks and fades. Avoid percentages in character.

Limits: Gameplay: absorption bonuses and Shield Strength figures are mechanics. They do not appear in character dialogue, and canon never states how much a barrier can take.

198.content:
Souls (also: soul, the soul, afterlife, the dead in Teyvat, ghosts and spirits, soul-stuff): Canon has no single doctrine of the soul. The recurring picture: the soul is what outlasts the body. After death it is meant to return to the Ley Lines, or in Natlan to the Night Kingdom, where it eventually loses its sense of self. A soul or memory that fails to go can linger as a ghost. Older belief sent the noble dead to cities on the moons.

Souls can also be split, marked, shared or stored: Zibai's soul was divided into fragments, Columbina left a piece of hers in a Luonnotar, Mitya's soul bears Ronova's mark, and Moon Wheels are said to be formed of soul-stuff. The Snegovik, Snezhnaya's fae, are said to be born with incomplete souls.

In universe: - Ley Lines: the standard destination. Ronova says that after the body dies the soul must return to the Ley Lines for death to be complete.
- Night Kingdom: in Natlan the dead go there; souls become Nightsouls and eventually merge into a sea of souls.
- Ghosts: souls or echoes that did not make the transition and linger on the surface.

- Irminsul: a record of everything in Teyvat; Nahida says the one way to enter it that she could not guard was through death.
- The moons: in an older age, boatmen ferried the noble dead to cities on the moons.

Ley lines and death: In the Wraith's Nocturne quest (7.0), Ronova explains that after the physical body dies, the soul must return to the Ley Lines for that person's death to be considered complete, and that her Authority covers the whole process, including guiding souls there. The Ley Lines of the Korolevskiy Theater had been modified by angels to make room for the souls of special creations, which hindered their ability to take ordinary souls: they could accept only two a day. Those killed by the Curse of Death were stuck in an afterlife that looked like the theater trapped in a blizzard.

Natlan night kingdom: When Natlan's people die they enter the Night Kingdom, a realm created by the Lord of the Night with Ronova's guidance that functions as Natlan's Ley Lines. There they eventually lose their sense of self and become one with the sea of souls. The souls in it are called Nightsouls, and Natlanese warriors draw on them for Nightsoul's Blessing.

Ghosts and echoes: Ghosts, also called spirits, appear throughout Teyvat. Flins, a Lightkeeper, says they are echoes of living souls: a portion of thoughts and memories that for certain reasons failed to enter the Ley Lines at death and so linger on the surface. They stay near fixed places and repeat words and phrases that mattered in life, and they are hard to reason with. In time their memories and yearning fade and slowly return to the Ley Lines.
