Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Natlan characters use Nightsoul's Blessing, Nightsoul Points and Nightsoul Bursts, mechanics drawn from the Nightsouls of the Night Kingdom. Moon Wheel users in Nod-Krai trigger Lunar Reactions through Moonsign passives, built on kuuvahki. Ghost NPCs are quest and world features.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): keep soul talk regional. A Natlanese character thinks of the Night Kingdom and Nightsouls; a Nod-Krai Lightkeeper of ghosts and the Ley Lines; a Liyue adeptus of arts and parting. Do not blend them into a single universal rule.

Limits: No source describes how reincarnation works, and no source lets an ordinary person talk to or free a soul at will.

A soul that has been dead too long or has lost its form is hard or impossible to help: in Natlan, dispersal is painful and unrecoverable, and in the Korolevskiy Theater, souls missing their window were lost for good.

199.content: In Natlan, the dead enter the Night Kingdom, where they eventually lose their sense of self and join a sea of souls. Their remnants are the Nightsouls that warriors draw on for Nightsoul's Blessing. Abyssal corrosion limits the kingdom's capacity, and shamans such as Citlali can open the gate for a lingering soul, which may refuse to enter.

200.content: Flins describes ghosts as echoes of the living: portions of thoughts and memories that failed to enter the Ley Lines at death. They repeat phrases from life, stay near fixed places and may respond strongly to anything tied to their memories, like the relit lighthouse in Nod-Krai. In time they fade and return to the Ley Lines.

201.content:
Spiritway (also: Spiritways, Spiritdoor, Spiritdoors): Spiritways are pathways of constantly flowing Phlogiston in Natlan. Anyone who can ride one moves swiftly in the direction of the flow. They first appeared in Version 5.0.

Only Koholasaurs, or people who have mastered the relevant technique, can use them freely, and the in-game text warns that not all Spiritways are complete or completely safe.

In universe: In-game text describes a Spiritway as a pathway formed by flowing Phlogiston. Riding it carries the traveller along the flow.

Spiritways may run one way or both ways; a route with portal-shaped ends is one-way, one without is bidirectional. A rider can join anywhere along the route and can leave at any point.

Who can ride: A rider must be in the Nightsoul's Blessing state. The People of the Springs and Koholasaurs (through Saurian indwelling) can ride naturally. Mavuika is not of the People of the Springs; after a fourteenth round of modifications Xilonen made at her request, Mavuika's flamestrider gained the ability to manipulate Phlogiston and use Spiritways.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): riding a Spiritway consumes no Nightsoul points, Phlogiston or Stamina.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): present a Spiritway as a glowing current of Phlogiston that sweeps a rider along at speed, bright when a Natlanese traveller uses it. Do not let an ordinary visitor ride one without a Nightsoul-based method, and do not invent a Spiritway network or origins beyond what canon states.

202.content: Spiritdoors are devices made by the ancestors of modern Natlanese using Phlogiston Engraving to imitate the techniques of the Spiritway makers. Interacting with one creates a Spiritway or brings an unstable one into being.

203.content:
Spread (also: Spread reaction, Dendro Spread, Catalyze Spread): Spread is a Dendro elemental reaction. First, Dendro and Electro meet and make Quicken, which leaves a Quicken Aura on the target. Any later Dendro attack on that target then triggers Spread, which gives that attack a flat damage bonus. The Electro counterpart is Aggravate, and the Dendro bonus is the larger of the two.

It debuted in Version 3.0 with Quicken, Aggravate, Bloom, Burgeon and Hyperbloom, the reactions introduced for Dendro. Unlike many reactions, it does not deal damage of its own.

In universe: Canon gives no in-world explanation for Spread. The pages read treat it as a combat rule, so it is best understood as plant energy riding on lingering charge and spreading through a target.

Gameplay: Gameplay: Dendro on a target with a Quicken Aura triggers Spread and adds a bonus to the attack that triggered it. Spread does not use up the Quicken Aura.

- Spread is a catalyze reaction, with Quicken and Aggravate. It adds an Additive Base DMG Bonus to the attack, so the bonus enters the damage calculation before the attack's other bonuses, CRIT damage, DEF and resistance apply.
- The base bonus is 1.25 times a level multiplier for Spread, against 1.15 for Aggravate. The wiki notes that Dendro attacks therefore receive a greater bonus than Electro ones.
- Elemental Mastery and certain artifacts raise the reaction multiplier; the two sources add together.
- The Quicken Aura lasts a number of seconds equal to five times the smaller gauge of the two elements, plus six.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show green energy running along crackling sparks, a vine-like glow spreading across a target and feeding the next strike. The attack hits harder, but nothing explodes by itself.

Limits: Spread needs a Quicken Aura first and only Dendro triggers it. It has no damage of its own.

The Quicken Aura fades with time. Bloom or Burning can use it up if Hydro or Pyro is applied.

Examples: Gameplay example: an Electro attack lands on a Dendro-affected enemy and starts Quicken. The next Dendro attack triggers Spread and hits harder, and the aura stays for more Dendro hits.

204.content: Quicken is the starting reaction of the catalyze family: Dendro on an Electro-affected target, or the other way round. It deals no damage and leaves a Quicken Aura that fades over time. Dendro attacks on it trigger Spread, Electro ones trigger Aggravate, and neither consumes it. See system.quicken.

205.content:
Stamina (also: Stamina bar, stamina meter, maximum stamina): Stamina is the yellow bar that drains when you sprint, dash, climb, swim, glide or make a charged attack. It is one pool shared by the whole party, starts at 100 and regenerates quickly when you stop.

Upgrading the Statues of The Seven raises the maximum, up to 240.

In universe: Stamina is a game mechanic, not something characters mention by name. Gameplay abstraction: it represents the physical effort of running, climbing and swimming.

Gliding with a wind glider costs only 3 Stamina per second, far less than sprinting at 18.

Gameplay: Gameplay: stamina is a shared party pool shown as a yellow bar beside the active character. It regenerates at 25 per second after 1.5 seconds of not spending it, and the bar hides itself when full. Switching characters does not restore it.

The bar is divided into sections of 100 Stamina each. Base costs, before any reduction, include:
- Dash: 18 per movement; sprinting: 18 per second.
- Climbing: continuous cost not listed (5 Stamina is the minimum needed to begin); a climbing jump costs 25 per movement.
- Swimming: 4 per movement; swim dash: 2 to start, then about 10.2 per second.
- Gliding: 3 per second while moving.
- Charged attacks: most sword characters 20; polearm 25; most claymore 40 per second; most catalyst 50.
Many characters' passive talents, some Constellations and certain dishes reduce costs, remove them or restore stamina. The Stamina Flower restores 80 Stamina.

Limits: Gameplay: stamina cannot exceed the current maximum, does not regenerate until 1.5 seconds after you stop spending it, and is not restored by swapping characters. Costs differ by action and, for charged attacks, by weapon type.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): do not quote numbers in scene. Show effort through breathing, slowing pace, and hands slipping on a wall. Characters with stamina-related talents can be shown as lighter on their feet, but do not make them tireless.

206.comment: Stamina: Statue of The Seven stamina upgrades
206.content: Offering oculi at a nation's Statue of The Seven raises that nation's statue level, and each early level also adds to the party's maximum Stamina (7 for the first two upgrades, 8 for the next seven). The maximum possible is 240. See the Statue of The Seven entry for the offering mechanic itself.

207.content:
Statue of The Seven (also: Statues of The Seven, Archon statue, Archon statues, Statue of Seven): Statues of The Seven are large stone statues of each nation's Archon, found across Teyvat. Legends say they were sculpted in the image of The Seven who sustain the world, and travellers pray to them for protection. In play they unlock the map, act as teleport waypoints, heal and revive the party, and swap the Traveler's element.

Offering oculi to a nation's statues rewards the player and raises the party's maximum Stamina.

In universe: Mondstadt's statue honours the Anemo Archon, Liyue's the Geo Archon, Inazuma's the Electro Archon, Sumeru's the Dendro Archon, Fontaine's the Hydro Archon, Natlan's the Pyro Archon and Snezhnaya's the Cryo Archon. Each statue shows a hooded figure holding an object shaped like the region's Vision. The in-game map text calls them monumental statues that "watch over" the land.

Statues seem to depict the Archon currently in office. The game's description reads: "Legends say they were sculpted in the images of The Seven who sustain this world. Travelers would pray for the statue's protection should they come across one, while it silently anticipates the arrival of a noble soul."
According to fairytales cited in The Blessings of The Seven, the statues originally had gem eyes that swallows carried off. Item text on the Anemoculus describes offering consolidated winds to a statue so that it can regain power it has lost.

Gameplay: Gameplay: each region's statues fill in map areas when first touched, unlock expeditions and teleport waypoints, revive fallen characters and heal the party. Interacting with a statue while playing the Traveler lets them change element to match that region.

Statue's Blessing: all statues share a pool of HP called Restorative Power. It refills at 1% of its maximum per 15 seconds (25 minutes for a full recharge). The maximum is 5,000 times the number of Statues of The Seven and Statues of the New Moon unlocked; the wiki gives 310,000 as the possible maximum as of Version 7.0 (55 statues of the Seven and 7 Statues of the New Moon). Each manual click heals a character by 10% of their maximum HP.
With "Auto-recover when nearby" enabled, fallen characters are revived at 35% HP for free, and party members below a chosen HP threshold are healed from the pool if you stay close for about 2 seconds. Statues also cleanse Bonds of Life and act as a source of warmth in Subzero Climate.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): statues are public landmarks where travellers rest, pray and wait for a safe teleport. Characters can say "pray to the statue" or "rest at the statue" without knowing about Restorative Power or oculi counts. Healing at a statue can be described as light and warmth rather than numbers.

208.comment: Statue of The Seven: Statues of the New Moon
208.content: In Nod-Krai, the Frostmoon Scions, who worship the Moon Goddess, built statues in the image of Columbina and placed them across the region, called Statues of the New Moon. They add to the Restorative Power pool like the Seven's statues in play.

209.comment: Statue of The Seven: Defiled Statue
209.content: Mondstadt long ago lost one of its Statues of The Seven. The Traveler later finds a Defiled Statue hanging upside down in the ruins in the quest Call of the Abyss.

210.content:
Stellar-Conduct (also: Stellar Conduct, Starlight Prism, Polestar Field): Stellar-Conduct is a Stellar Glimmer reaction from Snezhnaya. It happens when Cryo is applied to a target already affected by Electro, or the other way round, while a character with the matching Stellar Jubilee passive is in the party. It then replaces Superconduct. The reaction creates a Starlight Prism, which briefly turns the surrounding area into a Polestar Field.

It was added in Version Luna VIII (6.7), listed among the new systems of that version, and is the first of the two Stellar Glimmer reactions; Stellar Swirl followed in 7.0.

In universe: Canon says nothing in-world about the prism or the field. The only lore note concerns the whole family: Stellar Glimmer reactions are said to have been introduced to ancient Snezhnaya by Saarelainen, the Third Descender, and the wiki cites a Version 7.0 livestream for that. Do not treat it as detailed history.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Stellar-Conduct does no damage by itself. Damage comes only from character talents and constellations, and may be Cryo or Electro depending on the source.

After the reaction, the Starlight Prism lasts 7 seconds and keeps a Polestar Field around it. Inside the field, Cryo and Electro hits on enemies are recorded by the Prism; the hit that created it does not count. Every 4 seconds the count is reset and buffs lasting 4 seconds are given. Characters inside the field gain a Cryo and Electro damage bonus (20%, or 28% plus 1% per recorded hit if any hit was recorded, up to 12 hits). Enemies in the field lose 40% Physical RES. The reaction's base coefficient rises by 40% plus 5% per recorded hit, up to 12 hits.

Interactions: Stellar-Conduct replaces Superconduct when the matching passive is active, so Superconduct's usual outcome does not happen in that party. Stellar Swirl is the other Stellar Glimmer reaction.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show the Prism as a small star-like shard of light that hangs in the air above a frozen, crackling spot, with a faint ring of light around it. Allies inside it should feel steadier, and cold or heat should be easier to bear in Snezhnaya. Keep the scale at the size of a fight.

Limits: As of 7.1, no canon explains the reaction beyond its name and the family-level Saarelainen note.

Stellar-Conduct needs a Stellar Jubilee passive in the party. It is not a Lunar reaction.

211.comment: Stellar-Conduct: Starlight Prism and Polestar Field
211.content: The Starlight Prism is the object created by Stellar-Conduct. It lasts 7 seconds and sustains a Polestar Field, in which Cryo and Electro hits are recorded and then turned into party buffs. In the Snezhnayan open world, an unused Prism turns into a Prism Mirage that can be reactivated and then behaves like a Prime Ice Construct.

212.content:
Stellar Glimmer Reaction (also: Stellar Glimmer, Stellar Glimmer Reactions): Stellar Glimmer reactions are a small family of Cryo-related elemental reactions tied to Snezhnaya. There are two: Stellar-Conduct (Cryo with Electro) and Stellar Swirl (Anemo with Cryo). They take the place of Superconduct and Cryo Swirl only when a character with a matching Stellar Jubilee passive is in the party, and those characters are Stellar Linchpin users from Snezhnaya, or the Cryo Traveler.

The family was introduced in Version Luna VIII (6.7) with Stellar-Conduct, and Stellar Swirl followed in 7.0. Stellar Glimmer reactions also interrupt a specific attack from Snowland Fae and Aberrant Chimeric Monsters.

In universe: Canon gives the reactions almost no in-world explanation. The only lore note is that Stellar Glimmer reactions were introduced to ancient Snezhnaya by Saarelainen, the Third Descender. The wiki sources this to the Version 7.0 Special Program livestream rather than to quest text.

Stellar Linchpins are Vision-like objects from Snezhnaya that let users manipulate the elements. Fatui research, as shown in the quest "Should We Meet Again", links them to the remains of Saarelainen. The Fatui's idea is that impurities from his remains become fixed in place when a Linchpin manifests, hence the name. Users of elemental energy through a Linchpin often show a power that seems to come from beyond Teyvat.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): a Stellar Glimmer reaction needs a character in the party with a passive talent that converts specific Cryo-related reactions. The two reactions are Stellar-Conduct, which replaces Superconduct, and Stellar Swirl, which replaces Cryo Swirl. The passives are called Stellar Jubilee passives.

Enemies: Gameplay: Stellar Glimmer reactions disable certain attacks of Snowland Fae (Snegoviks, Vilas, Volkodlak Brutes) and Aberrant Chimeric Monsters, and a Leshy that is rooted and healing has its heart further exposed when a Stellar Glimmer reaction hits it.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): treat these reactions as a Snezhnayan quirk of elemental power, visible in the company of a Linchpin user. Frost, static or wind react in an unusually bright, starlike way, with sparkling light and a sense of weight. Scale it to a skirmish: no Stellar reaction should be shown as a world-ending force.

Limits: There are only two Stellar Glimmer reactions as of 7.1: Stellar-Conduct and Stellar Swirl. Do not invent further ones.

The reactions replace, not add to, the ordinary reactions, and require a Stellar Jubilee passive in the party. They are separate from the Lunar reactions, which depend on a Moonsign passive.

213.content: A Stellar Linchpin is a Vision-like object from Snezhnaya that lets its user manipulate the elements. Fatui research connects Linchpins to the dead Third Descender, Saarelainen, whose remains left impurities that fix in place when a Linchpin forms. What makes one appear is unknown. Linchpin users are the ones who enable Stellar Glimmer reactions.

214.content:
Stellar Jubilee Passive (also: Stellar Jubilee, Stellar Jubilee Passives, Stellar Jubilee Passive Talent): A Stellar Jubilee Passive is a passive Talent held by characters with a Stellar Linchpin, plus the Cryo Traveler. It is what lets Stellar Glimmer reactions happen at all: with a holder in the party, the matching Cryo reactions turn into Snezhnayan Stellar Glimmer reactions. Sandrone, Odette and Vesna each have one, as does the Cryo Traveler.

This is a gameplay label, not a term used by characters in the story.

Gameplay: Gameplay, not literal lore. With a holder in the party, a Superconduct triggered by any party member becomes Stellar-Conduct, and a Cryo Swirl becomes Stellar Swirl. The passive also raises the base damage of the converted reaction in proportion to the holder's ATK, and puts the holder into a "Radiance" state.

- Radiance: Stellar-Conduct applies when the holder is inside a Polestar Field, the area a Stellar-Conduct creates around its Starlight Prism.
- Radiance: Stellar Swirl applies for 8 seconds after a nearby party member triggers Stellar Swirl.
- Sandrone (Light of Rationalisme), Odette (Dance of Aurore) and the Cryo Traveler (Illusory Frostmirror) convert both reactions. Vesna (Splendid Prelude) converts Cryo Swirl only.

In universe: Gameplay abstraction; the story gives no in-world name for this passive. Canon context: Stellar Linchpins are Vision-like objects from Snezhnaya, and the Fatui's research ties them to the dead Third Descender, with users showing a power that seems to come from beyond Teyvat. In the Version 7.0 Special Program it was said that Stellar Glimmer reactions were introduced to ancient Snezhnaya by Saarelainen.

Holders: - Sandrone, Light of Rationalisme (released 6.7; the first holder, with Stellar-Conduct).
- Odette, Dance of Aurore (released 7.0).
- Vesna, Splendid Prelude (released 7.1).
- Traveler (Cryo), Illusory Frostmirror (version not verified).

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): treat the passive only as the reason that, around these characters, frost and lightning or frost and wind combine into a Snezhnayan star-like effect. Do not have characters name or discuss a "Stellar Jubilee Passive". Describe the result instead: a prism of light and a field of cold glittering light for Stellar-Conduct, a drifting vortex that bursts into frost for Stellar Swirl.

Limits: It enables only Stellar-Conduct (Cryo with Electro) and Stellar Swirl (Anemo with Cryo). Vesna's version covers Stellar Swirl alone. Do not extend it to other element pairs or to people without a Linchpin, apart from the Cryo Traveler.

215.content:
Stellar Linchpin (also: Stellar Linchpins, Linchpin, Snezhnayan star-Vision): A Stellar Linchpin is a Vision-like object from Snezhnaya. Like a Vision, it lets its bearer channel elemental power, but Stellar Linchpin users often show a kind of power that seems to come from beyond Teyvat. The Fatui believe Linchpins are tied to the remains of the Third Descender, and they study them for their weapon against the Heavenly Principles (Project Mistilteinn). Known users are Sandrone (Cryo), Odette (Cryo), Vesna (Anemo), Danica (Electro) and Mitya (Electro). Linchpin bearers can enable the Stellar Glimmer reactions.

It is not a Vision, a Gnosis or a Moon Wheel, and should not be called a Vision in narration. Sandrone, introducing the idea in 2026's Sunny Summer Fontinalia event (6.7), describes it as "a rare kind of Vision."

In universe: Visions are said to be a means of channelling elemental power for those who hold them. In Sandrone's explanation (as Marionette, in the 6.7 event), the same is true of Linchpins, with one difference: Linchpin users often exhibit a unique kind of power that seems to come from beyond Teyvat. What makes a Linchpin appear is not known.

Appearance in canon is gradual and personal. Sandrone found hers waiting on her workbench after her damaged body rebooted. Odette's formed in the "cold glimmer" backstage after a performance. Vesna's voice-over treats Linchpins as pretty collectible objects. Mitya wears his on a golden garter on the side of his left thigh, according to the wiki.

The third descender link: In Fatui research as relayed by Sandrone (Marionette), Stellar Linchpins are related to the Third Descender. When one manifests, impurities from his remains get fixed in place. In canon, the Heavenly Principles used his remains to create the seven Gnoses, which consolidated the Archon system; Visions come from that same system.

Project mistilteinn: Pierro of the Fatui explains in the Archon Quest "Wraith's Nocturne" (Act II, "Mistilteinn", 7.0) that elemental energy is the Human Realm's power, converted by the Heavenly Principles themselves, so using it against its creator would be futile. The Fatui therefore turned to the energy associated with the Third Descender and the Linchpins. By reverse-engineering Linchpins to extract their energy, they have what Pierro calls a source of "anti-Celestia energy."

Appearance: A Stellar Linchpin is shaped like a four-pointed star, similar to the shape of a Primogem, set in a star-shaped frame. Its casing resembles a Snezhnayan Vision's, with two rhombuses beneath the star. Mitya's is Electro and sits on his left thigh; Odette's was described as ice-blue, cold and almost weightless, no heavier than a frozen tear.

Known users: Sandrone (Cryo), Odette (Cryo), Vesna (Anemo), Danica (Electro), Mitya (Electro).

- Sandrone: Seventh of the Eleven Fatui Harbingers, artificer; her Linchpin appeared in the 6.7 event.
- Odette: prima ballerina of the Korolevskiy Troupe, Fatui; released 7.0.
- Vesna: Commander-in-chief of the Druzhna; Anemo user, released 7.1.
- Danica: head housemaid of the royal house.
- Mitya: scientist of the Royal Energy Commission.
Their personal stories belong to their own entries.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Characters with a Linchpin have a Stellar Jubilee Passive, which lets them enable Stellar Glimmer reactions. The Traveler (Cryo) has them too.

Limits: A Stellar Linchpin is not a Vision, and is not a substitute for a Gnosis. Sandrone herself uses it modestly: it supplies Cryo, which she uses to cool her systems, and she does not find that it solves problems for her. No canon text says a Linchpin makes its holder more than a skilled Vision-like elemental user.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): describe the Linchpin as a small, cold-looking star carried on the body like a Vision. Do not have an ordinary bystander name it correctly; it is a Snezhnayan matter, and Paimon needed Sandrone to explain it.

216.content: Gameplay: the passive talent shared by Stellar Linchpin users (and the Traveler as Cryo) that enables Stellar Glimmer reactions. Stellar-Conduct arrived in 6.7 and Stellar Swirl in 7.0.

217.content:
Stellar Swirl (also: Stellar Vortex): Stellar Swirl is a Stellar Glimmer reaction from Snezhnaya. It happens when Anemo is applied to a target already affected by Cryo, while a character with the matching Stellar Jubilee passive is in the party. It then replaces Cryo Swirl. It deals Anemo damage and leaves a Stellar Vortex that later bursts for Cryo damage.

It was added in Version 7.0 ("Everwinter Without Mercy"), after Stellar-Conduct in 6.7. The announcement presented it as a reaction that disturbs opponents and also helps exploration.

In universe: Canon says nothing in-world about the vortex. The only lore note concerns the family: Stellar Glimmer reactions are said to have been introduced to ancient Snezhnaya by Saarelainen, the Third Descender, citing a 7.0 livestream.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): on triggering, one hit of Anemo damage is dealt to the target, and a Level 1 Stellar Vortex appears for 3 seconds. After a delay the vortex bursts, dealing area Cryo damage.

Triggering Stellar Swirl a third time raises the vortex to Level 2, so that it bursts for more damage over a wider area. Three further triggers make it burst at once. For 5 seconds after any vortex bursts, the player's next jump is higher, which the announcement framed as an exploration aid.

Interactions: Stellar Swirl replaces Cryo Swirl in a party with a matching passive, so Anemo on a Cryo target no longer spreads Cryo to nearby targets. It does not replace Swirl with Pyro, Hydro or Electro. Stellar-Conduct is the other Stellar Glimmer reaction.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show Stellar Swirl as a small, bright whirl of frost and starlight that spins in place for a breath before it bursts outward. Anemo moves it, Cryo is what it leaves behind. Keep it to skirmish scale.

Limits: As of 7.1, no canon explains the reaction beyond its name and the family-level Saarelainen note.

Stellar Swirl needs a Stellar Jubilee passive in the party and an Anemo-Cryo pairing. It does not apply to other elements and is not a Lunar reaction.

218.content: The Stellar Vortex is the object left by Stellar Swirl. It lasts 3 seconds, bursts for area Cryo damage, levels up with repeated triggers, and boosts the next jump after it bursts.

219.content:
Superconduct (also: Superconduct reaction, Electro-Cryo reaction): Superconduct is the reaction that happens when Electro meets Cryo on a target, in either order. It is a burst of Cryo energy that damages everything in a small area and strips Physical resistance from the enemies it touches, so that sword, spear and fist hurt more for a while. It is a combat rule rather than a story event.

The damage is fixed by the reaction itself (the level and Elemental Mastery of whoever triggers it), not by the attack that set it off. The Cryo is not left on the target, so Superconduct cannot lead to a second reaction.

In universe: Canon does not explain Superconduct as a phenomenon of the world; it is introduced only through the game's Elemental Trial tutorial. Treat any in-world explanation as a scene decision, not as lore.

Outside battle the game shows the same pairing in the environment. Electro on water that Cryo has frozen shortens the freeze and leaves the water Electro-Charged, without area damage or Physical RES loss. Cryo on an Electro Crystal, or Electro on a Mist Flower, triggers a full Superconduct and hurts enemies nearby.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Superconduct deals AoE Cryo damage in a 5 m radius and reduces the Physical RES of enemies in the area by 40% for 12 seconds.

It is a transformative reaction with base coefficient 1.5 (from the wiki's Damage page), scaled by the triggering character's level and Elemental Mastery. It ignores the attack's ATK and cannot CRIT by default. Target resistance applies; DEF is practically ignored. Only the party applying the second element counts.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show Superconduct as a sharp crack of frost and static, a ring of shards or a snap of ice-blue lightning, followed by armour, hides or bone visibly weakening. Describe the effect as a short-lived weakness to blows, not a permanent wound.

Limits: Superconduct needs both Electro and Cryo; no other element pair produces it.

It applies no Cryo, so it cannot chain into Frozen, Melt or another Cryo reaction. Cryo on Electro-Charged water does not trigger it in the environment.

220.content: Superconduct is the Electro and Cryo reaction. It bursts with Cryo damage in a 5 m radius and lowers Physical RES by 40% for 12 seconds for enemies in the area. It leaves no Cryo behind.

221.content:
Swirl (also: Swirl reaction, Anemo Swirl, Pyro Swirl, Hydro Swirl, Electro Swirl, Cryo Swirl): Swirl is what happens when Anemo meets another element on a target: the wind catches that element and flings it outward, so everything nearby is hit or soaked with it. It works with Pyro, Hydro, Electro and Cryo, but not with Geo or Dendro. It is a combat rule rather than a story event.

Swirl deals its own damage in the swirled element (except Hydro, which only spreads Wet), based on the Anemo user's level and Elemental Mastery rather than ATK. Because it re-applies the element, it can set off further reactions on neighbouring targets.

In universe: Canon presents Swirl only through the Elemental Trial tutorial and gameplay text; no source read gives an in-world account of why wind spreads elements. Treat any explanation as a scene decision.

The tutorial wording is that when Anemo touches Hydro, Pyro, Cryo or Electro, the element in contact affects a larger area and can trigger other reactions.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Swirl applies the non-Anemo element to targets within a 6 m radius, except the target the reaction was triggered on. Pyro, Electro and Cryo Swirl also deal AoE damage of that element; Hydro Swirl spreads Wet and deals damage only to the triggering target.

It is a transformative reaction with base coefficient 0.6 (from the wiki's Damage page), scaled by the Anemo character's level and Elemental Mastery. It cannot CRIT by default and ignores ATK. The wiki separates this from Elemental Absorption, where an Anemo skill absorbs an element and deals ordinary damage of it; that damage uses normal attack stats.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show Swirl as a gust that grabs the burning, dripping, crackling or frosted thing and throws it out in a ring, with a scatter of sparks, spray or frost. The wind should visibly carry the element.

Limits: Swirl does not work with Geo or Dendro, and Anemo has no reaction with itself.

It spreads an element already present; it does not create one. The swirled element is not applied back to the triggering target, which lets the original target keep its own state.

222.content: Swirl is the Anemo reaction with Pyro, Hydro, Electro or Cryo. It spreads that element to everything within 6 m of the target and deals the element's damage (Hydro only spreads Wet).

223.content:
Talent (also: Talents, character talents, Combat Talents, Passive Talents, Ascension Passive): "Talents" is the game's interface term for the abilities of a playable character. Most characters have three Combat Talents (Normal Attack, Elemental Skill, Elemental Burst), two Ascension Passives and one Utility Passive. It is a gameplay abstraction: in the story people simply use their powers, skills or arts. Never have a character say "my Talent level is 9".

Talents are sorted into Combat, Ascension and Passive types. Some characters also carry extra passives tied to later systems (Natlan, Nod-Krai, Snezhnaya and Hexerei content).

In universe: Nothing found shows canon using "Talents" as an in-world category. What the interface lists as Talents are, in the story, a character's fighting style, Vision or Authority power, trained techniques and personal knacks.

The one Talent-adjacent idea with real lore is the Constellation: star signs said to govern the fates of Teyvat's people, whose unlocks upgrade a character's abilities in the game. Their lore and mechanics belong to the Constellation entry; here they matter only because two of them raise Combat Talent levels.

Combat talents: Every character starts with three Combat Talents unlocked at level 1: the Normal Attack (their main attack form), the Elemental Skill (no Energy cost, but a cooldown) and the Elemental Burst (usually costs Energy).

Combat Talent levels rise by spending Character Talent Materials ("talent books", from the weekday Domains of Mastery of each nation) up to level 10, with the usable cap set by the character's Ascension phase. Talent levelling starts at Ascension phase 2 (around character level 40 and Adventure Rank 25).

Ascension passives: Two passive Talents unlock with Ascension: the 1st Ascension Passive (phase 1, character level 20) and the 4th Ascension Passive (phase 4). Most improve a Combat Talent.

Ascension Passives cannot be levelled up. Their effects often do not show on the Combat Talent's own attribute screen.

Passive talents: Besides Ascension Passives, a character has a Utility Passive (also called an Exploration Talent), unlocked on acquisition; the Traveler has none. It does something outside combat: cooking, crafting or forging bonuses, reduced stamina cost, faster movement, expedition bonuses, resource markers on the map, or not startling certain wildlife.

Alternate Sprints replace normal sprinting and are listed as an additional passive. They cost 10 Stamina to start and 15 per second afterwards, against 18 and 18 for a normal sprint; they cannot be levelled.

Gameplay: Gameplay (labelled mechanics, not lore): the Normal Attack, Skill and Burst buttons use the matching Talent, and an Alternate Sprint is used if the character has one. Talents largely decide a character's role in a team; Elemental Resonance and other team bonuses sit on top of Talents rather than inside them.

Limits: Do not give a character a numeric Talent level, a cooldown readout or an Energy bar in dialogue, and do not call story powers "Talents".

Talents are not Visions or Constellations. A Vision (or Authority) is the source of an element, while Talents are what a character does with it. The Traveler has no Utility Passive.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon): describe Talents through their fiction, such as a signature move, a technique that needs a pause before reuse (the cooldown), or a finishing move that drains the user (the Burst). A passive can show as a habit or knack. Stay with what canon shows the character doing.

224.content: A Combat Talent starts at level 1 and rises to level 10 with Character Talent Materials, limited by Ascension phase. Constellations that raise a Talent by 3 levels lift its cap to 15.

225.content: Each character apart from the Traveler has a Utility Passive from the start, giving a non-combat benefit such as a crafting refund, a stamina reduction, a movement bonus or map markers.

226.content:
Teleport Waypoint (also: Teleport Waypoints, Portable Waypoint, Sub-Space Waypoint, fast travel): Teleport Waypoints are devices found across Teyvat. Once the Traveler unlocks one by touching it, it can be chosen on the map to fast travel there. In-world, they are old, odd structures the locals have grown used to without knowing what they are for; to the Traveler, a foreigner, their use is obvious.

The map text puts it this way: Teyvat's people regard them as ancient gimmicks and are accustomed to them despite not knowing their purpose.

In universe: Canon gives no explanation of who built Teleport Waypoints or how they work. Treat them as unexplained ancient machinery that happens to carry the Traveler between places.

The Portable Waypoint's item text offers a different note: it describes a pocket-sized item that makes a temporary Waypoint, able to connect with the ley lines at least enough to bring about teleportation, and adds that the real principles behind Waypoints are not yet fully understood and that the hope is that using them has no undesirable side effects. That text speaks from inside the world and treats the Waypoints as known devices, which does not match the "ancient gimmick nobody understands" framing.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Waypoints are map markers that are unlocked by interacting with them, then used to fast travel. Statues of The Seven, Statues of the New Moon, domains and High-Speed Transit Lanes also work as teleport points once unlocked.

They also act as respawn points when a whole party falls, clear accumulated Sheer Cold, Withering decay and Abyssal decay from harmful climates, recharge the Lumenstone Adjuvant in The Chasm: Underground Mines, and replenish Phlogiston in Natlan. Most are unlocked by touching them once the area is lit up on the map, which is done through a Statue of The Seven or Statue of the New Moon, or through quest progress.

Limited event waypoints: Event-only areas have had their own Waypoints that can no longer be reached: 7 in the Golden Apple Archipelago during the 1.6 event Midsummer Island Adventure, and 10 when it returned in 2.8; 10 in the Darkness-Encroached Enkanomiya in 2.5; 9 in the Veluriyam Mirage in 3.8; and 17 in Simulanka in 4.8. Some were unlocked automatically during the event quests or once the event ended.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): inside a scene, the Traveler stepping onto a Waypoint and arriving elsewhere is fine as a shorthand for travel. Locals treat the devices as familiar background furniture, not as technology anyone can explain. Do not claim Waypoints run on ley lines, belong to a particular civilisation, or that ordinary NPCs can use them, as canon supports none of these.

Limits: Canon gives no builder, no mechanism and no in-world rules. Katheryne's fast-travel remark in Inazuma is not a basis for treating other characters as able to teleport. Fast travel is a gameplay convenience; most Fatui, Knights and travellers are shown crossing Teyvat on foot, by ship or by other means.

227.content: The Portable Waypoint is an alchemy-made consumable that creates one temporary Teleport Waypoint at the user's location. It lasts seven days and only one can exist per world. Its item text calls it a pocket-sized item capable of connecting with the ley lines enough to cause teleportation, and notes that its convenience for Vision bearers comes with the caveat that the real principles of Waypoints are not fully understood. Sub-Space Waypoints are furnishings for the Serenitea Pot that look different but work the same way.

228.content:
Vaporize (also: Vaporize reaction, Pyro-Hydro reaction): Vaporize is what happens when Pyro and Hydro meet on a target. It deals no damage by itself; instead the attack that triggers it hits much harder, as if the water flashed to steam under the blow. It is a combat rule rather than a story event.

Which element lands second decides the strength: a Hydro hit on a Pyro-affected target is amplified more than a Pyro hit on a Hydro-affected target.

In universe: Canon presents Vaporize only through the Elemental Trial tutorial and gameplay text. No source read for this entry gives an in-world account of why it amplifies damage, so any in-world explanation is a scene decision.

The tutorial wording is simply that when Pyro meets Hydro, the triggering Hydro or Pyro damage receives a bonus, and that the bonus is larger when Hydro is the trigger.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Vaporize multiplies the damage of the triggering attack by 2 if Hydro is applied to a Pyro-affected target, and by 1.5 if Pyro is applied to a Hydro-affected target.

It is an amplifying reaction, like Melt. The multiplier is further increased by a percentage based on the triggering character's Elemental Mastery plus any Reaction DMG Bonus from effects such as artifact sets. Vaporize deals no damage of its own, so a talent that only applies an element and deals no damage gains nothing from it.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show Vaporize as a burst of hissing steam when water strikes fire, or when flame scorches a wet foe, followed by a visibly harder hit. Keep it about the force of the blow, not extra effects.

Limits: Vaporize needs both Pyro and Hydro, and it never creates damage on its own.

It does not turn into another reaction and does not involve Geo, Anemo, Electro, Cryo or Dendro.

229.content: Vaporize is the Pyro and Hydro reaction. It amplifies the triggering hit: x2 when Hydro triggers it, x1.5 when Pyro does. It deals no damage of its own.

230.content:
Vision (also: Visions, God's Eye, Eye of God, allogene, allogenes): A Vision is a jeweled amulet, worn on the body, that lets its bearer channel one of the seven elements directly. The bearers are called allogenes: people with unusually strong desires or ambitions who might one day ascend to Celestia and become gods. Most people never receive one. A Vision does not give mastery, only the channel; the power still has to be practised.

Common belief says the Archons hand Visions out, but canon states they do not pick recipients and do not know who receives them. Visions are given as a form of acknowledgement by Celestia, and they cannot be destroyed.

In universe: A Vision links a person to an element (Pyro, Hydro, Anemo, Electro, Dendro, Cryo or Geo). Venti told the Traveler in the Prologue that Vision holders are allogenes who might ascend one day. A bearer has some elemental sensitivity and can sense their element more keenly than other people.

Bearers are not automatically skilled: ability varies from Shenhe freezing a tsunami to young Yaoyao channelling power through a device. Overuse causes exhaustion that only rest cures.

Allogenes: Allogene is the in-universe term for a person who is fit to hold a Vision. In the original Chinese, Japanese and Korean the word is the same as the game's title and means roughly "primordial god" or "original god". Allogenes may ascend to Celestia, though most do not.

Venti, in Ending Note, calls Vision holders allogenes who could one day ascend. The Archons are not the givers, so an allogene is not a favourite of their own nation's god, although many believe otherwise. Allogenes who achieve their goals are said to cause the gods to receive an abundant gift (Neuvillette's Vision story).

Receiving: There is no sure way to get a Vision. They arrive during crises and fights, at moments of resolve or revelation, after major accomplishments, or on an otherwise ordinary day. Survival alone is not enough.

The wiki sorts the cases into three groups. Some bearers receive it directly before or on them while conscious, in a crisis, a resolution or after an accomplishment. Some notice it nearby, or find it later among their belongings, after making a resolution. Others receive it while asleep or unconscious, during or after a crisis, unrelated to one, or after reacting in a dream. A person worthy of a Vision either receives a new one or reactivates a nearby Masterless Vision.

Losing: Visions cannot be destroyed, according to Keqing's research, but they can be separated from their owners, willingly or by force. A person parted from their Vision may lose the ambition that drove them, and sometimes memories too; others show no ill effect.

Masterless: When an allogene dies, their Vision goes dull, losing colour and power, and becomes a Masterless Vision. A Masterless Vision rarely resonates with someone new.

A Masterless Vision wakes when a person's desire matches the original owner's, and takes on the same element as before. Kaedehara Kazuha briefly woke his late friend's Electro Vision while deflecting the Raiden Shogun's Musou no Hitotachi, using it alongside his own Anemo Vision. It went dormant again afterwards. Most people think two Visions at once is impossible.

Related objects: Delusions, Gnoses, Moon Wheels and Stellar Linchpins are separate things; do not call them Visions.

A Gnosis is a chess-piece-like object that embodies the Heavenly Principles' control of Teyvat, with only seven made. Archons use their powers without needing it, while humans usually depend on a Vision. A Delusion is a Fatui device that lets anyone wield elements, more powerfully than a Vision and at serious cost, such as lost vitality. Bearers of a Vision or elemental ability resist the effects better.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): treat a Vision as a personal symbol of an unmet or fulfilled ambition. Characters may touch or glance at it when they speak of their goals. Do not make it a mere weapon permit: mention how its owner received it, and let characters differ in attitude, from pride to unease.

231.content: An allogene is a person with a desire strong enough to hold a Vision and, in principle, to ascend to Celestia. Venti defines Vision holders this way in Ending Note. The word is the same in Chinese, Japanese and Korean as the game's title.

232.content: A Vision whose owner has died. It loses its colour and elemental power and is an empty husk until someone with the same desire resonates with it. Kazuha's temporary use of his friend's Electro Vision is the best-known case.

233.content: Inazuma's decree under the Raiden Shogun collected Visions from their holders. Losing a Vision had varied effects on memory and ambition, and Electro Visions stopped appearing during it. Full details belong to the Decree's own entry.

234.content:
Witchcraft (also: witch magic, Hexenzirkel magic): Witchcraft in Teyvat is not a single taught discipline. The word points at the witches and mages of the Hexenzirkel, the circle of powerful women founded by the adventurer Alice, whose members practise astrology, alchemy and other arts, and at titles such as Lisa's "Witch of Purple Rose". Their powers are shown through individuals, from a near-omnipotent sorceress to members with no magical training at all. The game also uses "Hexerei" as a team-bonus label for characters tied to the circle.

This entry describes the magic the witches use. The circle itself (history, members, island) belongs in the Hexenzirkel faction entry, and the individual practices have their own entries: Alchemy, the Art of Khemia and Mystic Arts in Teyvat (for astrology and hydromancy).

In universe: Hexenzirkel members are called witches or mages, but the label is loose. Alice, the founder, is a long-lived polymath with alchemy, astrology, engineering, magic and medicine among her skills. Barbeloth reads fate by astrology. Rhinedottir practises the Art of Khemia. Nicole is an angel who survived the fall of her kind. Octavia travels the Sea of Stars. Two members, Andersdotter and I. Ivanovna N., never had any magical or combat training.

Members use code letters and epithets: Alice (A, the Merry-Witch), Barbeloth (B, the Seer-Witch), I. Ivanovna N. (J, the Tricksy-Witch), Andersdotter (M, the Story-Witch), Nicole (N, the Memory-Witch), Octavia (O, the Wander-Witch) and Rhinedottir (R, the Sage-Witch). Alice's criterion for inviting members was that they be "interesting"; moral virtue was not required. Members appear in several forms, notably as Dodoco-shaped dolls in witch hats with individually coloured tails, and some voices reach the world through phonographs, teacups or lanterns.

Members: Seven founding members are named in canon. Alice and Barbeloth are the circle's best-known active practitioners; Nicole is a playable angel; Octavia created the pocket realm Miliastra Wonderland and has visited at least 1,896 planets; Rhinedottir is one of the Five Sinners of Khaenri'ah and, after merging with Naberius, the Ruler of Life among the Four Shades. Andersdotter (deceased) was an acclaimed writer; I. Ivanovna N. (deceased) became a powerful Snezhnayan politician and the first Mayor of Snezhnograd.

Practices: - Divination: Barbeloth pioneered hydromancy (a subclass of astrology) and is said to be able to read the fates of whole nations and the world; Mona practises it as her student. Barbeloth's case of oracles is tied to the Lunar Arcana.
- Alchemy and life-making: Alice practises alchemy; Rhinedottir's Art of Khemia creates life and does not entirely conform to Teyvat's rules.
- Life extension: Alice can extend a human's lifespan through magic (Andersdotter refused).
- Realm-making: Simulanka, the Imaginarium Theater and Miliastra Wonderland are all creations of members, and members are said to rewrite fate in some cases. Andersdotter helped Simulanka's creation and rewrote fate for her child, Durin.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): "Hexerei" is a team-bonus label. After completing Witch's Homework, a character becomes a Hexerei character, and the Hexerei: Secret Rite team bonus applies when the party has two or more of them. The Little Witch's Dictionary, received from Alice, is the item that issues the homework. The wiki lists Albedo, Klee, Mona, Venti, Durin, Varka, Nicole, Lohen, Fischl, Razor, Sucrose and Prune among them.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): present witchcraft as personality plus craft, not a spell list. A Hexenzirkel scene is playful on the surface, with teacups, tea parties and Dodoco-shaped messengers, while the power underneath is ancient and world-scale. Different witches should feel different: Alice's enthusiasm, Barbeloth's teasing way with fate, Nicole's silence, Rhinedottir's coldness and strictness (as Albedo remembers her).

Limits: No unified rules exist. Each member's feats are personal, from Alice's island-moving to Barbeloth's readings; some members have no magic at all. Even the powerful are limited: Barbeloth, for instance, warns that revealing fate too readily spoils the future.

235.content: The Hexenzirkel is the circle of witches that Alice founded; its members use code letters A, B, J, M, N, O and R and epithets such as Merry-Witch, Seer-Witch and Sage-Witch. They gather for "formal tea parties" and have used a secret island above Falcon Coast. Their purpose is mysterious. See the Hexenzirkel faction entry.

236.content: Astromancer Barbeloth Trismegistus, the Seer-Witch (B), is the master hydromancer who taught Mona. She is Alice's friend and rival, and an elderly woman in blue witch attire. She mapped the fates of all living things in Simulanka and, according to Mona, can read the fortunes of nations and the world.

237.content: Alice (A) is a travel writer, adventurer and the founder of the Hexenzirkel, a long-lived elf-eared woman at least 500 years old, and Klee's mother. Albedo calls her a near-omnipotent sorceress. She appears chiefly as a voice in a Dodoco, phonograph or teacup, and first appeared in person in the 6.2 Nod-Krai quest. See her own entry.

238.content: Gameplay: the Hexerei team bonus rewards parties of characters who have completed Witch's Homework. Alice gives the player the Little Witch's Dictionary in the quest "Unexpected Commission". This is a game label, not proof of Hexenzirkel membership.

239.content:
Witch's Homework (also: Witch's Homework quests, The Little Witch's Dictionary, Witch's Eve Rite Passive, Witch's Eve Rite): Witch's Homework is a system from Version 6.2 in which The Little Witch's Dictionary hands out tasks, made by the Hexenzirkel's mages, to friends of the Traveler. Finishing a character's task makes them a Hexerei character and unlocks a bonus Talent for them, the Witch's Eve Rite Passive. In story terms the "homework" is the witches' long-range preparation to help Mondstadt in a future time of need.

The Traveler gets the dictionary in the world quest "Unexpected Commission", set at the Knights of Favonius Headquarters in Mondstadt.

In universe: Alice, a Hexenzirkel mage, wrote the dictionary with other mages. The title is a disguise: it claims to explain the storybook "The Little Witch and the Undying Fire", but the two books are unrelated and the dictionary is really full of tasks tailored to individual readers. The item text says it was made by the witches and is "actually filled with homework tailored by the Hexenzirkel for each reader."

Alice explains the reason in "Unexpected Commission": the Hexenzirkel promised Varka at the Tripartite Conference that in Mondstadt's greatest time of need the mages would return and help. Rather than appear out of nowhere, they chose to lay groundwork over time (a line she attributes to "M", the Hexenzirkel's Andersdotter). The tasks, drawn up after looking into Barbeloth's scryglass, are about striving toward a common goal, overcoming obstacles with trusted companions and becoming better people. Alice stresses this is preparation, not a warning that something is about to happen. Item and event text add the motto "To defy the current is to learn."

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): each Witch's Homework quest belongs to one character. The player must own that character and have them at level 70 or higher. Finishing it makes the character a Hexerei character and unlocks their Witch's Eve Rite Passive, which also changes some of their Talents and Constellations.

Most of these enhancements work only when at least two Hexerei characters are in the party, which switches on the Hexerei: Secret Rite Team Bonus (own entry, Hexerei). The dictionary is a gadget that lets the player view and accept the tasks; the same quest also invites Razor, Fischl or Sucrose to the party from the event menu.

Release note: Witch's Homework arrived in Version 6.2, "A Nocturne of the Far North" (2025-12-03), together with the Hexerei Team Bonus. A later system with the same flavour, Witch's Revelation, followed in 6.7 (own entry).

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): treat the homework as the Hexenzirkel's gentle, slightly mischievous coaching, framed by Alice's cheer. A character who "has done their homework" has simply taken on a task from the dictionary with companions. Do not suggest Hexerei characters are all witches or Hexenzirkel members, or that a specific disaster is coming to Mondstadt.

Limits: Canon text seen names only the dictionary's framing, the Hexenzirkel's promise and the broad themes of the tasks. The system does not say who is a witch, and "Hexerei" is a gameplay label. Do not invent additional rules for what each homework contains beyond what each character's quest shows.

240.comment: Witch's Homework: The Little Witch's Dictionary
240.content: A 5-star gadget received from Alice in "Unexpected Commission" and reusable. Its item text calls it a dictionary created by the witches that claims to explain the storybook "The Little Witch and the Undying Fire" but is in fact filled with homework tailored by the Hexenzirkel for each reader, and ends with the words "To defy the current is to learn. Embark on your journey with your companions and seek the crown of elevation!" The dictionary's contents are not related to the storybook.

241.comment: Witch's Homework: Witch's Eve Rite Passive
241.content: The additional Talent a Hexerei character gains after finishing their Witch's Homework. Most of what it enhances, in the character's Talents and Constellations, applies when at least two Hexerei characters are in the party under Hexerei: Secret Rite.

242.content:
Witch's Revelation (also: Witch's Revelation Passive, Revelations by Chance): Witch's Revelation is a system from Version 6.7 in which the fortune-teller Barbeloth's Witch's Revelation Case holds oracles for particular characters. Completing a character's Witch's Revelation quest unlocks an extra Talent, the Witch's Revelation Passive, and enhances some of their Talents and Constellations. It is the sequel in spirit to Witch's Homework: Barbeloth and Alice are again behind it.

The Traveler gets the case in the Fontaine world quest "Revelations by Chance", near the Court of Fontaine.

In universe: Barbeloth, a powerful fortune teller, is running a small divination stand just outside the Court of Fontaine, and tells the Traveler that as a Descender from beyond the world the Traveler's own fate cannot be predicted by most fortune tellers, herself included. She recently glimpsed an omen, followed it and caught threads of fate and the faces of their owners, who are all people the Traveler knows.

Alice, who is helping with the divination, joins through Barbeloth's Dodoco-shaped stand-in and wants to hold a party for everyone involved. Barbeloth considers invitations delivered by messenger birds likely to disturb fate and refuses, but allows the Traveler to bring the people to the stall because their fates are already tied to the Traveler's. The case itself, per item text, once belonged to Barbeloth and contains every oracle, those already revealed and those still to come; she says she prefers a future with secrets still to unfold.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): each quest belongs to one character. The player must own that character at level 70 or higher. Finishing it unlocks the Witch's Revelation Passive and changes some Talents and Constellations. The Passive also lets the character enter the Radiance state under certain conditions.

The Passive allows a character to enter Radiance: Stellar-Conduct while inside a Polestar Field. A Polestar Field is created by the Starlight Prism that forms when the Stellar-Conduct reaction (Cryo with Electro, a Stellar Glimmer reaction) is triggered. The "Revelations by Chance" quest follows "Song of the Dragon and Freedom" and gives the player the case, 20 Primogems, Hero's Wit and Mora.

Release note: Witch's Revelation was introduced in Version 6.7, "Sunny Summer Fontinalia" (Luna VIII, 2026-07-01). Its announcements presented it as the witch's new divination, with an accompanying new reaction and Talents. Witch's Homework (6.2) is the earlier system of this kind.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): play Barbeloth as dry, teasing and unwilling to explain fate in full, and Alice as warmly enthusiastic about parties. A character with a Revelation has simply been "read" by Barbeloth; do not claim the reading predicts their death or doom, since canon seen here states no specific outcome. Do not claim Barbeloth can read the Traveler's fate.

Limits: Canon gives only the stand, the case, a rough sense that fate is being nudged, and the seven character quests. Do not invent contents of the oracles, the cause of the prophecy, or the nature of Radiance. Barbeloth stays out of the way of the Traveler's future, which she says she cannot see.

243.content: A 5-star reusable gadget obtained in "Revelations by Chance", used to view and accept Witch's Revelation tasks. Its text says the case once carried by Barbeloth has reached the Traveler, and holds all the oracles, both revealed and not yet opened, with Barbeloth declining to say whether they could steer fate.

244.content: The additional Talent unlocked by a Witch's Revelation quest. It enhances some of the character's Talents and Constellations and allows entry to the Radiance: Stellar-Conduct state within a Polestar Field.
